July 25-The Prime Minister-The following proposed motion:-That the resolution adopted by this house on the 14th day of June, 1960 and reading as follows:
"Resolved, that a humble address be presented to Her Majesty the Queen in the following words: To the Queen's most excellent majesty:
Most gracious sovereign:
We, Your Majesty's most dutiful and loyal subjects, the commons of Canada in parliament assembled, humbly approach Your Majesty, praying that you may graciously be pleased to cause a measure to be laid before the parliament of the United Kingdom to be expressed as follows:
An act to amend the British North America Act, 1867.
Whereas the Senate and House of Commons of Canada in parliament assembled have submitted addresses to Her Majesty praying that Her Majesty may graciously be pleased to cause a measure to be laid before the parliament of the United Kingdom for the enactment of the provisions hereinafter set forth:
Be it therefore enacted by the Queen's most excellent majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the lords spiritual and temporal, and commons, in this present parliament assembled, and by the authority of the same, as follows:
1.	Section ninety-nine of the British North America Act, 1867 is hereby repealed and the following substituted therefor:
"99. (1) Subject to subsection two of this section, the judges of the superior, district and county courts shall hold office during good behaviour, but shall be removable by the Governor General on Address of the Senate and House of Commons.
(2) A judge of a superior, district or county court, whether appointed before or after the coming into force of this section, shall cease to hold office upon attaining the age of seventy-five years, or upon the coming into force of this section if at that time he has already attained that age."
2.	This act may be cited as the British North America Act, 1960, and the British North America Acts, 1867 to 1952, and this act may be cited together as the British North America Acts, 1867 to 1960.
3.	This act shall come into force on the first day of March, nineteen hundred and sixty-one.

EQUALIZATION OF QUOTAS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I ask leave to move, seconded by the hon. member for Kootenay West, the adjournment of the house- under standing order 26 to discuss a question of urgent public importance, namely the large number of marketing points in western Canada still on a 6-bushel quota and the need for urgent action at this time to assure that quotas will be equalized, thus enabling each producer to deliver his fair share of grain.
I believe that this question is of very great urgency, Mr. Speaker, because the end of the crop year is approaching. This is July 27 and the crop year ends on July 31, just four days from now. There have been commitments from the government on previous occasions that every possible step would be taken to make certain that delivery quotas were equalized by the end of this crop year. The importance of this, I should like to 
point out, is that by equalized quotas the farmers are given the same opportunity to deliver grain and therefore an equal opportunity with their neighbours to the same kind of income return.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: EQUALIZATION OF QUOTAS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit me to ask a question which might help me in determining the urgency of debate? Is this a matter within the administrative jurisdiction of the Canadian wheat board?

maintopic: EQUALIZATION OF QUOTAS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: I would say quickly yes to that, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: EQUALIZATION OF QUOTAS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Then the urgency the hon. member suggests is that-the end of the crop year is when?

maintopic: EQUALIZATION OF QUOTAS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: At the end of this month, four days away.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: EQUALIZATION OF QUOTAS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: And the importance of it is that-?

maintopic: EQUALIZATION OF QUOTAS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Once we pass the end of the crop year all the quotas return to zero and the farmer has no opportunity whatever to

deliver grain. It is illegal to deliver grain on the present quotas on August 1, which is a very few days away. If equality in the delivery of grain, therefore, is to be brought about, immediate action is necessary so that this can be accomplished within the next few days.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: EQUALIZATION OF QUOTAS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: I take it that the jurisdiction to set quotas after the end of the crop year is just as it was before; there is no change?

maintopic: EQUALIZATION OF QUOTAS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: EQUALIZATION OF QUOTAS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
I feel I have heard sufficient to enable me to deal with the matter. The question is, of course, one of urgency of debate that we have to consider under rule 26. The hon. member raises a matter which is of undoubted importance, and of particular importance to the producers of grain who are making deliveries. But the problem I have to consider is whether or not there is a lack of opportunity in this house to discuss this matter which is so urgent as to warrant our interrupting a very full program at a time of the session which I think puts a rather severe onus on anyone who attempts to move the adjournment under standing order 26.
In my view there has been opportunity throughout the session to discuss the administration of the deliveries of grain, and if I am not mistaken the Canadian wheat board is under the administrative responsibility of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, whose estimates are to be called within the next day or two, so I would not think it appropriate to give leave to move the adjournment.

maintopic: EQUALIZATION OF QUOTAS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: If I might make a very brief comment on that-

maintopic: EQUALIZATION OF QUOTAS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: EQUALIZATION OF QUOTAS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: The quotas will be off; the opportunity will be gone. It will be too late.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: EQUALIZATION OF QUOTAS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: I appreciate what the hon. member says, but there will be an opportunity to discuss it when the estimates are being considered.

maintopic: EQUALIZATION OF QUOTAS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, I claim the right to deal with the central question at this time for the benefit of the house, as to whether or not this is sufficiently urgent that it is necessary to initiate a debate at this time. A question has been raised very properly by Your Honour as to whether or not there will be an opportunity, in your own words, within the next couple of days to debate this matter.
Now Mr. Speaker, if the Minister of Trade and Commerce would bring on his estimates then that could be done; there would be no urgency if the trade and commerce estimates 79951-0-444J
Inquiries of the Ministry were brought on immediately. If they were initiated, as the minister announced last night, at the tail end of the session, then these quotas will be down to zero and there will be a great injustice done to the western producers; that is why it is urgent.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: EQUALIZATION OF QUOTAS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: I took those matters into consideration in the course of making my ruling.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, since the crop year for the delivery of grain in western Canada expires on July 31, I would like to ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce whether he is in a position to make a statement with regard to quotas on grain.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON DELIVERY AND QUOTA POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the quota situation in the western prairies is better this year, I think, than in any year since the quota arrangement was put into operation. There are 2,007 stations on the quota distribution system. As of July 25, 1,879 or in other words roughly 94 per cent were on the 7-bushel quota, leaving roughly 6 per cent, or 128 stations, on the 6-bushel quota. This is a development which under the supervision of the wheat board has been pursued this year in an endeavour to equalize the quota distribution system as much as possible.
I have not had a communication today but I will be hearing from the wheat board, and I would expect that the number of stations on the 6-bushel quota has again been reduced, so that substantially all stations out west are on an equal basis. This is a major achievement, and every possible effort is being made during the closing days of the crop year to bring all stations up to the 7-bushel quota and to provide box cars in order that the grain may be moved rapidly. I doubt if a better showing has been made in any of the years since the wheat board has been operating.

speechtext: This question comes up every year. The wheat board with its long experience has reached the conclusion that it is unwise to extend the quota distribution system too far into the new crop year. Every year this question has come up I have examined it with the wheat board and asked them for their experience in years gone by. They have taken the stand that when they can reach the 7-bushel quota as they are doing this year it is adequate for marketing purposes. In certain areas, depending on the arrival of box cars, a few days' grace are permitted, but then the year closes and the new quota goes into effect for subsequent deliveries of grain from the new crop. Yes, Mr. Speaker. Yesterday the hon. member for Laurier stated that meat inspectors in the city of Montreal had not received pay for their overtime work for the last three months. He asked if I would inquire into the situation and advise him why this condition exists. The hon. member also stated that it was his understanding that the overtime was paid by the packing houses in which the meat inspectors worked.
In fact the overtime is not actually paid by the packing plants. If a plant engages in overtime operations a charge is made against the plant to cover the approximate cost of the overtime worked by the meat inspectors, but the payments from the plants are deposited to consolidated revenue. The actual overtime payments to the inspectors are made from the regular departmental vote in accordance with civil service regulations.
Those regulations provide for overtime worked by a civil servant to be liquidated as compensatory leave at any time up to the end of the following month if staffing permits, or failing that, for the payment of overtime. For this reason payment for overtime worked in any one month cannot be made until after the end of the following month.
Cheques covering overtime payments to health of animals staff in the Montreal area for April have been sent out, and it is anticipated that payment for overtime worked during May will be made within a week.

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
The house resumed, from Tuesday, July 26, consideration in committee of Bill No. C-58, to amend the Combines Investigation Act and the Criminal Code-Mr. Fulton- Mr. Flynn in the chair.
On clause 13, section 33-Mergers and monopolies.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: Shall the amendment to clause 13, section 33, carry?

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I was in the middle, or perhaps not in the middle; I should say I was at the beginning of a statement about this matter which has been occasioned by the observations which were made by the Minister of Justice just before I began.
In order to put what I now have to say in perspective I should like to recall just what it was I did say in my introduction last night. What I said was that, as the hon. member for Ottawa West had shown in his masterly reading of the proceedings of the banking and commerce committee, the government had made a firm and unqualified decision, and announced it to the committee, not to do anything about this problem. The government had decided that because the restrictive trade practices commission was carrying on an investigation into an export problem in British Columbia, no attempt should be made to meet the requests of the fisheries council, of the forest industries and of the metal mining industry which were

presented so ably, and I think so convincingly, to the committee, and whose views were put on the record at such length by three hon. members on the other side of the house last evening in speeches the urgency of which was apparent to all who listened to them.
That was the situation right up until the last meeting of the banking and commerce committee. At that point, sir, as I explained earlier yesterday, thanks to the courtesy of the committee and because of my absence on that Monday morning, the committee resumed its sittings in the afternoon and I introduced an amendment to clause 15 of the bill. I should like very briefly to draw to the committee's attention now the reason I gave then for doing so. This will be found at page 747 of the proceedings and evidence of the banking and commerce committee for July 18. Quite a way down the page the chairman is reported as follows:
Perhaps we could go on with Mr. Pickersgill first-
Then I am reported as having said:
I have an amendment I would like to move, seconded by Mr. Tardif. But before doing so, I would like to say that some of my friends and I on this committee were very much impressed by the representations that were made to the committee by a number of witnesses, expressing the hope that if the act was to be amended, as was the government's intention, some express provision could be put in the act to make it abundantly clear what everyone, I think, recognizes has always been in fact the situation, namely, that the purpose of the legislation was to prevent combinations within Canada respecting trade within Canada and was not intended, in any way, to cripple our export trade; and that if certain types of combination or arrangements were necessary for the promotion of our export trade they should not be hampered by this legislation.
Now I recognize-as I am sure every member of the committee does-how frightfully difficult it is to draft provisions which will make that position abundantly plain to the courts, without, in any way, having any ancillary effects or any serious ancillary effects which would enable it-as we thought might be the case with some of these new provisions that it is suggested should be inserted into one of the other sections, section 32-to be used as a cloak for combinations that are clearly intended to be against the law.
However, we do think that an amendment might be made to clause 15; and I must say that in proposing this, I am not absolutely wedded to this particular wording. It is the best, with such resources that were available to my friends and myself, we were able to come up with at the moment; but we would certainly appreciate any suggestions from any member of the committee that might make it more acceptable to the government.
In the present circumstances, when it is perfectly evident to everyone that we are not going to have the kind of sellers' market for our exports we have enjoyed most of the time since the second world war, we do think it is of the utmost importance, in the national interest, that we should do everything possible and everything reasonable both to promote our exports and to make sure,

by the laws of our country, that we are not providing any obstacles, even if only psychological obstacles, that can easily be removed.
When I made that statement I was authorized to speak, and was speaking, on behalf of my friends here in the house. That was the position, after very careful consideration of this very ticklish and difficult problem, that the Liberal party had decided to take on the matter. We had decided to take the view that even though there might be some slight risk -and we recognize there might be some risk -that such combinations for the purpose of promoting Canadian exports might become a cloak or might have effects in the domestic market which would by themselves be undesirable, for the greater good of the country and indeed the greater good of a majority of consumers, in view of the tremendous extent to which the income of the Canadian people, particularly of the people in certain provinces, is dependent upon our income from exports, that balancing the two, one against the other, it was in the national interest to move such an amendment.
Now, sir, I am glad to say that the arguments we put forward there and, perhaps more than the arguments, the knowledge that the Liberal opposition had taken this up officially as its policy, caused the government to change its mind. Let no one be under any illusion about this matter. The amendment we are now considering, for which we intend to vote and which I admitted quite frankly yesterday is better drafted than mine was, would not have been offered at all if it had not been for the stand I was asked to take in the banking and commerce committee on behalf of the Leader of the Opposition and our party on the last day the committee sat on this bill.
In view of some of the things that were said yesterday, and in view of the obvious efforts of certain members opposite to get on this band wagon and try to make it appear that in some way this was their doing, I think the record ought to be set straight.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
The hon. member has made what he alleges to be a statement of fact, and I wish to say at once and immediately following what he has said that his statement of fact is not correct. It is not the case that this amendment would not have been offered had it not been for the motion made in the committee by the Liberal opposition. It is true that I had indicated in the banking and commerce committee throughout that I was concerned as to the appropriateness of offering an amendment while a case was still under discussion before the commission and up to the time I had last previously spoken in the
Combines Investigation Act banking and commerce committee I had not been able to see my way around the difficulties.
But I had indicated clearly that we were considering the matter. I was considering the matter. I had discussions with a number of our own members, and I told them that the government and the minister were prepared at any time they could come to the conclusion that an amendment could be drafted to submit one to the house. I repeated that on the day the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate has referred to, Monday, July 18. It was not by any means simply because he had presented an amendment that we came to the conclusion that an amendment could be drafted and that we were justified in drafting and submitting an amendment at this time.
My hon. friend probably will not accept my assurance on this point. No more do I accept his statement or interpretation of why this amendment is now before the house. But hon. members on this side, with whom I had discussions both before and after he offered his amendment, will know perfectly well the truth of what I say, and they will know that it is a gross exaggeration, and immodest exaggeration for the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate to say it is simply because he moved this amendment that the house now has one before it from the government.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, may I ask the minister, who now so passionately claims the parentage of the idea of this amendment, why, having regard to the months, indeed, the year or so when they were drafting their amendments, this idea did not appear in the bill when it was submitted to the house after all the consideration that was given to the matter by them?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: This and all sorts of other ideas occurred to us.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: You did not put it in the bill.

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, from the activities of both the Liberals and the Conservatives. I know they are very excellent band wagon climbers, and therefore it is doubtful whether the accusation of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate should be treated too seriously. However, I think he did place some of the facts before the banking and commerce committee in a little different light. Trade is an extremely important matter because we depend so much upon it; but because we have been in so much difficulty since approximately the middle of 1957 in our trading relationships with other countries I hope the Conservative government and its supporters will not think that the change now being made in this legislation is a cure-all for our trade problems. I trust they will not
7028	HOUSE OF
Combines Investigation Act be content to rest upon the false base that this amendment will assist to any measurable extent in increasing our trade with other nations. It only needs a cursory glance at the provision to see that it cannot be considered a cure-all for our trading problems, and that more aggressive measures must be taken by government departments, notably the Department of Trade and Commerce, to increase our exports to other countries.
Our objections to this amendment have been placed on the record clearly and I do not think there is any point in going over them again. I am only making these remarks because the feeling might develop that we have done something which will cure our trading problems or as a result of which they will solve themselves. We need a much more aggressive attitude toward trade. There are other problems and difficulties which have not been thought of or have been glossed over. We are encountering difficulties because of the activities of other nations, and those interested in export trade have used these difficulties as a basis for arguing that they should be exempted from the application of the Combines Investigation Act so far as their export activities are concerned.
A reading of the briefs presented by organizations which appeared before the banking and commerce committee and advocated that their export activities should be exempted from the provisions of the act indicates that they used arguments which were not valid. Perhaps they are most succinctly put by Mr. Nicholson, president of the council of forest industries of British Columbia, who appeared before the committee on June 22 along with representatives from the fisheries council of Canada and the Canadian metal mining association, to which reference has been made.
As found on pages 292 and 293 of the proceedings of the committee Mr. Nicholson put forward what I think were false arguments to promote an exemption under the combines legislation. I should like to refer to them in order to indicate that we need to tackle our trade problems in other ways than by means of the Combines Investigation Act. Mr. Nicholson referred to the letter read by Mr. Hyland of the fisheries council which was written by the Japanese cartel on fish, and near the bottom of page 292 he said:
I was shocked at the letter as I am sure you were-the letter that Mr. Hyland read here today which was written by the Japanese fishing cartel and written approximately eleven months ago. I am sure the words burn themselves in your mind just as in mine-"We have not yet fixed our final price for the sale of our salmon in the world market: we give you a tentative price and as soon as the Canadians and Americans have fixed their price we will give you ours." How in the world


are you going to fight in world markets where 50 per cent of the products of the forests of British Columbia are being exported and one third of the income coming into this country from the sale of our exportable commodities coming in from the sale of Canada's forest products, if we cannot meet the competition coming in from foreign countries?
Then my colleague the hon. member for Port Arthur asked a question:

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: Could the witness give us the parallels in the timber industry to the Japanese salmon industry? I do not think that is contained in the brief.

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I cannot give it to you for Japan, but I can give it to you for Russia. Prior to the war, and in fact up until 1954, Canada was Britain's leading supplier of softwood products-lumber, shingles and material of that kind. That is, as late as 1954 it was the leading supplier. By 1957, Canada's share of the United Kingdom imports had dropped to 14.7 per cent and Canada's position was that of fourth place supplier of products to the building industry in Britain. We had been replaced successfully by Sweden, Finland and Russia. During this period when Canadian sales were dropping off the Soviet of Russia had increased her sales from one tenth to one fifth of the total of United Kingdom's softwood importation. In the case of the Swedish and Finnish importers they were trading at a profit.
Notice the distinction there, and it is developed later on, that the Swedish and Finnish exporters were operating at a profit. The implication is that the Russian exporters were not operating at a profit, and this is developed later on. I continue the quotation:
Their objective was to make a profit, but their operating costs were lower because wages were lower. That was not so in the case of Russia, when they came in and took that market. I am reliably informed by an official of the Department of Trade and Commerce-this can be checked by reference to the minister or other officials of that department-that the Russian technique in invading the British market is that they will come in with a particular type of lumber which is in demand, and even though the lumber may be needed at home in Russia, they will quote to supply the whole demand at a price that is better than the Canadian price for a particular kind of lumber.
I imagine when he uses the word "better" he means lower.
It is even better than the Swedish and Finnish prices in some cases. Then if you repeat the order they will give you a further reduction. That is not done by any cartel. That is done by a government trade agency. Does that answer your question?
He went on then to deal with another matter. I should like to point out that our problems and difficulties in the export markets could not be even partially solved by the amendment before us now to exempt export activities from prosecution under the Combines Investigation Act. 1 refer particularly to our difficulties in so far as the Soviet union is concerned. Mr. Nicholson has pointed out here the manner in which the Soviet undertook to export lumber to Great Britain,

thus cutting into the amount of lumber that had been exported from Canada prior to 1954. I have not been in Russian nor have I worked in industry there, so I have no personal knowledge of these facts, but it is generally understood that Russian exports are controlled by a state organization. They have no worry about profits; they have no worry about costs of production; they have no balance sheets which have to be totalled up. The cost of production can be absorbed by society as a whole. The selling price in the world market means, in fact, relatively little.
Canada cannot possibly compete with the Soviet union in world markets because of the system under which the Soviet operates. When it comes to Sweden and Finland undercutting us because of wages, that is another matter. The natural implication of Mr. Nicholson's remarks is that if wages are the only factor, then one solution perhaps would be to reduce wages here to a point where they were comparable with wages in other countries so that we would be able to compete on price. Alternatively we could increase our productivity to the point where we were producing units of wood or whatever it was, say 1,000 board feet of lumber or squares of shingles, at lower per unit costs and then we would be in the position where we could compete. None of these things can be accomplished by an amendment to the Combines Investigation Act.
If it is desired to tackle this question through the Combines Investigation Act, then this amendment fails to meet the problem because it refers only to those exemptions connected with price conspiracy under section 32, which covers agreements between so-called competing corporations. There is no reference whatever in the minister's amendment to the activities of monopolies in the export market. It is true that a monopoly, because there is only one corporation, would have difficulty in conspiring with itself to set prices. It is an automatic action that a monopoly takes to meet these conditions. However, a monopoly does operate in the export markets, and that fact is not dealt with in this amendment.
Then we have to consider the problem of the merger of two companies in the export field. Suppose there were two competing firms, Anglo Canadian Fish Company and B. C. Packers or any other two fish companies or two lumber companies, which entered into a conspiracy in relation to the export of articles, and that conspiracy had no deleterious effects on the domestic market. For the sake of argument let us say that the conspiracy with regard to the export market was protected by the proposed amendment
Combines Investigation Act to add subsections 4 and 5. These two companies merge, and they are still engaged in export trade. There is then no conspiracy, because the companies have merged and there is now a monopoly or price leadership situation. What is the position of these companies in so far as the Combines Investigation Act is concerned?
As I understood the amendment originally proposed by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate in the banking and commerce committee, it dealt with mergers and monopolies as well as price conspiracies. It appeared to cover the whole range of illicit corporate activities with which this Combines Investigation Act seeks to deal, apart from the resale price maintenance and price discrimination provisions. These are matters which I think should be dealt with and answered.
There was one other matter which I raised and upon which I was not satisfied with the answer given to me by the minister last evening. I think perhaps the point I made is still valid and I should like to reiterate it. In paragraph (c) of the proposed subsection 5 which is before us it is stated:
(e) has restricted or is likely to restrict any person from entering into the business of exporting articles from Canada;
My contention was that there could be some conflict between that provision and the provision in subsection 3 of section 32, which reads in part as follows:
-has restricted or is likely to restrict any person from entering into or expanding a business in a trade or industry.
It was my thought that the minister should have included these words "or expanding a" also in (c). The minister maintains that these things are dealt with in other paragraphs. He mentioned that paragraph (a) contains protection in this regard when it talks of reduction or limitation of the volume of exports of an article. I believe he also made reference to paragraph (b) in which the language used is:
-has restrained or injured or is likely to restrain or injure the export business-
It could be interpreted to mean that if it prevented the expansion of business, therefore it meant to restrain or injure the export business of any domestic competitor who is not a party to the conspiracy, but I think for soundness and for sense my suggestion should be followed. There is a connection between the activities of corporations which conspire to set prices, to limit production, to limit supply or to do any of the other things prohibited in subsection 1. There is a connection as to whether these activities are in the export field or whether they are solely in the domestic field or whether they are
7030	HOUSE OF
Combines Investigation Act all one or a bit of each. There is a close connection. It is very easy for the activities in the export field to spill over into the domestic field and to injure trade or commerce in Canada internally as a result of their extraterritorial designs and activities.
I think it would be best to place these words "or expanding a" in the subsection so that it reads substantially the same as subsection 3. It is dealing with the same thing. The minister started off in subsection 4 by relating it to a paragraph in subsection 1 and saying that in any prosecution under the subsection a corporation may be convicted if certain things take place. This is the same argument or the same thought that is expressed in subsection 2 where it refers to a prosecution under subsection 1. They are relating to subsection 1 in each case. Subsection 3 indirectly relates to subsection 1 because it talks about entering into or expanding a business. I think these things all have a connection with the basic prohibition against conspiracy to injure trade, fix prices and so on.
Accordingly in this regard, Mr. Chairman, I think I should formally place this matter before the committee by moving:
That the amendment be amended by deleting in line 2 of paragraph (c) the word "the" between the words "into" and "business" and substituting therefor the words "or expanding a".
In my view this amendment would bring the provisions or the words in line with those in subsection 3. I do not think it would have as great a tendency to leave the court in the position of wondering whether we meant something different, as to the activities of a conspiracy and their effect on the export market, from what we meant when we were talking about a conspiracy to exchange statistics internally and its effect upon the domestic market.
If it is the intention of the minister that he means something different, then that is another case entirely, but it appears to me that we are getting at the same thing. It seems to me that the minister wants to ensure that if there is a conspiracy on the export market, this should not have any detrimental effect internally, within the nation. Such being the case I think this suggestion should be adopted, for the sake of consistency and in order to make it easier for the courts, if a case such as this gets into the courts, to determine just what parliament was getting at when it drafted these particular words.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
This matter was discussed last night and I explained that we had thought about this problem. It is not as though the amendment was drafted without a good deal of care and consideration. We came to the


conclusion that the problem of preventing somebody from expanding in an export industry is covered by a combination of subparagraph (a) and subparagraph (b) of this proposed subsection 5. Surely if the arrangement would prevent the expansion of some business in the export field it is covered by (a), because the arrangement is likely to result in limitation of the volume of exports of an article; and if it was not covered by that provision, the arrangement would certainly have the effect of restraining or injuring or being likely to restrain or injure the export business of a domestic competitor under (b). Hence in either one or both of those subsections the problem has been covered.
As I said last night, what my hon. friend seeks to do, whether or not there is any necessity or any logic for it, is to force words which are applicable to one situation into a section or subsection applicable to another situation. Following that course would result in the complete distortion, twisting and straining of words, or else a framing of amendments beyond their natural and proper meanings or their logical and proper compass.
I therefore oppose the amendment, not because I say the objective sought to be achieved is undesirable, but because the objective is already achieved. It has been carefully considered as a matter of drafting, and I submit that the hon. member for Skeena does not base it upon any sound proposition. He would be sound if he could show that it was not covered, but he cannot do that. He is simply basing it on the proposition that exactly the same words should be used in all parts of the bill. That is a proposition with which I cannot agree.

So, for all these reasons

That refers to the reasons the minister had given up to that time:
-but mainly because I do not think this amendment, as worded, contains sufficient safeguards in the interest of the domestic market and of consumers in Canada, I suggest the amendment be not accepted.

speechtext: Of course, Mr. Chairman, those words are on the record; but it might interest the hon. member to know that before had moved his amendment I had had meetings, as we believe it proper to do although my hon. friends opposite seem to think it is improper, with hon. members supporting the government who were on the banking and commerce committee. speechtext:
I shall be glad to try to answer that question briefly. I have other evidences of paternity, so I am not particularly interested in the paternity of legislation. Of course I do not object to the minister talking to his friends. I talk to my friends, and I think it is very proper that the minister should talk to his. However, I will still go on believing, despite what the minister said this afternoon, that what the hon. gentleman said that day in the committee is what he really meant. But that is another matter.
To try to answer the hon. member's question briefly, I think it was always intended that, except in so far as a combination had a detrimental effect on competition in Canada, this legislation should not apply to the export industry. In any case I always understood that was the intention, I always thought it was the intention, and I think it should be the intention. I also think that in a period when we do not enjoy a seller's market in the export trade the balance as between the
Combines Investigation Act promotion of exports and making absolutely sure that domestic consumers all the time get their supplies is very often on the side of maintaining our export markets and our income in order to buy goods at all.
Anybody who represents mainly fishermen and loggers, as I do, will appreciate what I mean. I am quite sure I said that yesterday and the minister said that too. I do not think either of us is absolutely sure that this amendment will work out entirely satisfactorily. I think it is a pretty good effort at drafting. It seems to me it represents pretty accurately the kind of thing that most of us in the banking and commerce committee and most of the witnesses who were concerned about this matter really wanted. It may be that some of those in the export business would not be as much concerned about consumers as we are, but I think it is a pretty good effort and a splendid tribute to the skill in draftsmanship of the officials who prepared this amendment.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: As far as I am concerned I hope it works out not to the disadvantage of consumers and I hope it does something to help our export industry. At the same time I thoroughly agree on one point with the hon. member for Skeena, with whom I do not always agree. If I thought this amendment was going to lull the government into feeling that it has now solved the export problem, I would have grave misgivings about it. I believe this government has a terrible problem which it is not facing up to in maintaining and expanding Canadian exports, but that is no reason for not supporting anything that I think may be of some little help in this regard, and that is what I think this may be.

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
To return to the general discussion, I was not able to be present yesterday when considerable time was spent on this subject. I wish to reiterate my support of the stand of the hon. member for Skeena. We are not going to support this amendment. I scrutinize the statement made yesterday by the minister when he introduced this. I am curious about some things he said, especially in relation to the question asked by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. At page 6971 the minister is reported to have said:
-in the light of the current position in international trade, the situation of Canadian industry is declining-
At page 6972 the minister is also reported as having said:
However concerned we may be about the welfare of our industry in the export field, it still remains the primary concern of all of us to protect the interests of the Canadian consumer at home.

Combines Investigation Act
I do not suggest there is any conflict, but as the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate indicated some are not concerned enough about the trade position. We feel the only way we can keep a reliable economy alive is through promoting export trade. I come from an area that is even more dependent upon the export trade than the minister's area. I might add that probably my constituency puts more into the export trade in terms of returns to the country than the whole province of Newfoundland.
Therefore when I take a position with regard to this particular amendment I do so with some care because I know there are five pulp and paper mills, mostly in the export market, in my constituency alone, plus several substantial base metal mines. The reason I do not wholly agree with the amendment is that I think it only partly meets the problem. It seems to me it has relevance particularly to the British Columbia fishing and lumber industries. It seems to me that this amendment will be more useful perhaps just to the mines or to the tender susceptibilities of the British Columbia lumber industry than to the salmon packing industry. I am not sure about the effect it may have in so far as the base metal mining industry is concerned, which seems to me to be the other large group that had a representation to make when they appeared before the committee on this matter.
I am not an expert in the international trade field, but I look at the copper situation. I understand that the world price tends to be determined to quite an extent by what is in effect a cartel, in which Canadian copper producers play some part. I think everyone who has been following the crises in Chile and the labour troubles of the Congo, on account of nationalism, recognizes that this factor has been discussed a number of times: What is going to be the effect of the particular troubles there upon world copper prices? My understanding is that several large companies which have a certain kind of interlocking relationship do play a very important part in so far as the world price is concerned.
There is a parallel to the copper situation which is recognized, and that is the question of oil. I think it is recognized here that price determination is not a matter of national groups putting copper or oil on the international trade market. This is what the minister emphasized in his speech, and this would be one means of enabling Canadian industries to face what is in effect a national type of organization. He mentioned Russia, Japan and other types of cartels.
I should very much like to hear from the minister what effect this may have in giving encouragement to Canada to play a greater


part in these international oil and copper agreements which, at least from many points of view, are looked upon as not very bad. In other words, there are two kinds of cartels operating in the international field to where our products may be going. One is the national type, or it may now be the regional type as a result of the European common market, and there is also what you might say is the industrial products kind. It does seem to me that this amendment considered this particular possibility.
I do not think that the mining industry, from what I know of it, has ever been particularly stopped by this legislation. I should like to have more specific examples before I would like their position to be taken into consideration. I understand that up until recent years International Nickel to quite an extent, because of their overwhelming share of the market, did, I will not say set the price because the price has some relationship to demand, but they were in a very powerful position and we have heard arguments in the past that they controlled the market. Therefore it seems to me that this amendment is to a degree a sop, or a go-ahead, to two specific groups, namely the British Columbia lumber industry and the salmon industry.
I do not know much about the salmon industry, but I do know what the British Columbia lumber industry does to the lumber industry in eastern Canada and in northern Ontario in particular. Here again it is always a competitive swirl. What happens when the British Columbia lumber industry has difficulty in marketing its lumber or plywood in Britain? I think the minister is aware of it. Immediately they begin to dump some of their surplus on the eastern Canadian market; and because of its very volume and certain transportation rates they have, they are able to put our spruce producers or our plywood producers almost completely out of the market. Our people who produce lumber or pulpwood in northwestern Ontario are delighted when the British Columbia lumber people have an export market, because it means they are not ruining our people.
I make this point. There is a very close connection between the export market and the domestic market in terms of the way British Columbia dominates all the rest of the lumber industry in Canada once it finds its export market has shrunk. This underlines to me the very close connection between the export and the domestic markets and the correlation of price and volume to demand. Therefore it does not seem to me that this amendment is an adequate way to face up to the general problem.
I think we are going to move to the stage where we shall have to have, despite the

fact that the lumber industry particularly is against it, some kind of marketing arrangement, with government sponsorship and government participation, which will enable us to meet the challenge in more fields than just salmon or lumber. We have already a recognition of this in fields such as wheat, where there is no problem of the exporter being ruled as a cartel, a combine or a conspiracy because the sale of wheat is government sponsored.
I would be delighted if the minister would give some indication that in the very severe trade picture facing Canada, the government is giving some consideration to sponsorship or participation in a way which will allow us to gear for great expansion in our exports, and certainly to the effect that there would be no penalty for such a conspiracy. But until we know more of the relationship between the export position and the domestic position, it seems to me that this is an inadequate measure.
I do not think the minister would go ahead with this amendment unless he had looked at all the problematical circumstances with respect to our export trade. As I understand it, the largest single export is pulp and paper, or more specifically newsprint. What effect is this amendment going to have in the newsprint field? As I understand it, at the present time the price of newsprint is not a wide open matter. There is very little price fluctuation, and in so far as the United States market is concerned, while there is a certain amount of negotiation and a certain amount of spill of production at a lower price, in the main the price is one that I would not say is set by a conspiracy or coalition but is set by what might be called the big manufacturers in the field.
I remember there were charges several years ago when the head of Abitibi, I believe, D. W. Ambridge, announced an increase in the price of newsprint. There was a big holler from the Americans. I believe a United States senator said that here was an indication of the kind of conspiracy that went on in Canada to milk or bilk American buyers. There surely is quite a close relationship between the price set by the industry for newsprint that goes to the United States and the price that is paid within the domestic market.
I should like to know, for example, the price the Winnipeg Free Press pays for the paper it may buy from the mill at Pine Falls, and the price the mill at Pine Falls gets for the paper it ships to the midwestern United States. I do not believe anyone has ever made a great issue about it, but I think the export price determines the domestic
Combines Investigation Act price completely, and that the only difference is in the packing and transportation cost of moving a roll of newsprint from Pine Falls to Winnipeg compared with moving a roll to St. Louis, Missouri, let us say.
When the largest and most profitable of all our export industries is in a position where the relationship between the domestic price and the export price is almost identical, except for the difference in transportation costs, I wonder whether in effect we have not got in this industry just what this amendment sets out to clear. In that sense I intend to argue that the amendment is not necessary. I think it was partly the view of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate that he had always thought this would hardly apply in the case of something that was a great earner for Canada. These points indicate to me that this is a much larger and more complicated problem than this amendment can deal with.
It was interesting to note that to an extent the minister agreed with this view. He talked in his speech about the economic problems involved and how complicated the whole matter was, and said that perhaps they should wait for a report from the restrictive trade practices commission. Before we even think about a report from the restrictive trade practices commission I think we should consider something much broader, the whole role of the Canadian government with respect to export trade.
We are avowedly socialists, I believe, and I would expect our point of view to be markedly different from the Liberal or Conservative position. The minister referred to the crisis in export trade and our declining position. I was pleased to hear him say this, because it seems to be in conflict with the somewhat rosy picture we occasionally get from the Minister of Trade and Commerce. It is my view that the situation is serious enough that as a nation we must have a much grander sweep in the export trade picture, and that this amendment is more or less a temporary provision that does not make enough sense for us to be able to support it.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose at six o'clock on Saturday the Prime Minister was speaking on the subject of Canadian participation in the oil and gas resources of northern Canada as well as the mining properties of the future in northern Canada. I should like to take this opportunity of repeating to the committee one remark made by the Prime Minister, which can be found on page 6874 of Hansard, in the right hand column. The quotation is as follows:
But what the minister has done in connection with oil has been to take one of the major steos ever taken in Canada to provide that this vast but exhaustible resource shall provide not only for economic expansion in our country, and ensure an exploitation of them which we can only consider in imagination, but at the same time maintain for Canadians their sovereignty over their country, because no nation worthy of the name can maintain its political sovereignty unless it has every regard for the maintenance of its economic sovereignty.
I read this statement by the Prime Minister to give me the opportunity of emphasizing again that since this government took office, not only have we moved to allow insurance companies to mutualize themselves when they are threatened by an invasion of foreign investment, but we have also passed the national energy act which ensures that before any monopoly or quasi-monopoly is given to any pipe line company, that company will have to satisfy the national energy board that full opportunity has been given for Canadian participation in the ownership of the shares of that company.
The other day I read to the committee the United States regulations, which indicate how that country tries to ensure that no alien shall have control over the resources on the public lands of their country. Their legislation goes back to 1930. As the Prime Minister pointed out, this great concern of the people of the United States over outside investment coming into their country and taking over their natural resources caused them to put these regulations in their statutes 30 years ago, and we only moved in that direction in Canada in 1959.
These regulations in the United States are identical to the regulations in Canada. The thing to remember is that all they had to worry about at any time in their history was the fact that about 15 per cent of the investment in their resources was foreign investment, while the foreign investment rate in Canada is much higher. This has caused considerable concern and anxiety among Canadians. As a result, we believe that we have

7037 moved in a major way to give Canadians the chance to participate in the ownership of the resources of this country. We believe, furthermore, that this step was long overdue in this country.
At this time I should like to point out that the regulations in connection with oil, gas and mining only become effective at the time the company goes to ownership. It does not affect them during the exploration period. We simply make certain that every company taking out an exploration lease knows that before it goes to ownership there will have to be an opportunity for participation by Canadians. I should like now to read another of the mining regulations of our country dealing with the processing of these resources. This is regulation 101, and reads:
All grants and leases issued under the provisions of these regulations are subject to the provision that all ores or minerals mined from locations described in such grants or leases shall be treated and refined within Canada so as to yield refined metal or other product, suitable for direct use in the arts without further treatment: in default whereof the grant or lease issued for such lands shall be and become null and void:	and the
said lands shall forthwith revert to and become revested in the crown freed and discharged of any interest or claim of any person or persons whomsoever and shall be open to disposal in such manner as the chief may decide:	iron ores
produced in excess of smelter requirements from locations situated on any of the islands of Hudson bay in the Northwest Territories may, however, be exported for treatment.
I have read this regulation 101 into the record in order to make it absolutely clear that the thinking does not confine itself just to ownership of the mine taking the resources out of the ground. I think it also indicates the government's thinking that there has to be some control over the use of those ores extracted from Canadian soil. Obviously it is to our advantage wherever possible to have these ores processed or refined to the maximum in Canada.
I point these things out in order to make absolutely clear which way the government is moving in regard to meeting the anxiety of the Canadian people over the fact that so much of their natural resources has gone into the hands of foreign investment. As the Prime Minister said on Saturday, we welcome foreign investment here, but we should like them to set up Canadian subsidiaries in which Canadians can invest and have ownership and control, and also we should like the Canadian subsidiaries to act with the national interests of the Canadian people in mind and not those of their parent corporations in whatever country they are situated.
This is a major step forward. I pointed out on Saturday that this is just a start. I have to say at this time that I think this brings into clear focus some of the differences that
Supply-Northern Affairs exist between the vision of development of Canada for Canadians by Canadians that this government has and the vision which was described on Saturday by one of the opposition members as the Liberal vision. In view of the fact that, in the case of oil and gas, between 80 per cent and 87 per cent of the reserves of Canada are now under foreign control and ownership, the question that we must ask ourselves is this. Where were these people with the vision of the Liberals these last 25 years? We have to ask ourselves, what did they do to reconcile the differences or clashes that occurred, as the Leader of the Opposition said1, between this question of Canadian control and obtaining international investment? These are the questions which I think we have the right to ask the opposition. The debate we had here on Saturday in my opinion was a good1 debate, because it brought out in an objective way, and in a way that has been fair I think on both sides, the clear issues which are before us on this subject.
I think it is right for me to say, at least it is an opinion of mine, that the people of Canada ruled on this matter in 1957 and 1958. They thought that the government which had been here for 22 years sitting idly by while these resources had gone into foreign hands did not deserve the confidence of the people of Canada, and they therefore put in power the government led by the present Prime Minister.
The Liberals say they have a vision. I say they have no vision, because if we allowed this type of thing to continue for which they stood, Canada would soon be in a position in which, no matter what governments did, her resources would be gone unless there was a willingness to go into the policy of repudiation and taking over of contracts just as other countries have done.
The previous government is on record as saying that nothing could be done; that it was not the place of the federal government to do anything; that these resources belonged to the provinces and nothing could be done by the federal government to be helpful. I say that we have done something, and we intend to go on giving a lead. We know that the resources in the provinces belong to the provinces, and there will be no interference on our part; but I also suspect that as the provincial governments read these regulations we have put into effect dealing with our resources in the north, they will be following suit; because if they do not follow suit the people of the provinces will force them to do so by changing governments. We want to give Canadians a real chance to participate in the ownership of their resources. We have taken the lead as a federal government in

Supply-Northern Affairs those areas over which we have jurisdiction, and we expect that the provinces will follow.
A second theme that arose during the debate on Saturday and on which I want to say a few words is this question which the Leader of the Opposition, with his fondness for parallel structure, put forward in this way. He said the Conservative vision was a mirage, that it was a series of declamations and not development. He said it was words, not action. I should like to join issue with the Leader of the Opposition on this point with a series of things that this government has done. But before I do that I should like to remind the committee of something that occurred in 1955 and 1956, namely the submissions of various groups to the Gordon commission which made a series of reports in 1955 and 1956. For example, I should like to start with a document that the Leader of the Opposition used, namely a brief presented to the Gordon commission by the commissioner of the Northwest Territories. The date of his submission was November 22, 1955.
I am going to read into the record the recommendations made by the commissioner of the Northwest Territories; then I shall have something to say about what was done by the previous administration and what was done about these recommendations by the present administration. I am quoting from page 23. The heading of the section is "Ways and Means of Encouraging Economic Development". I will start at paragraph 3 on this page:
Before discussing how the costs of transportation can be brought down, the first question to be decided is whether it is desirable, at this stage of Canada's economic development, to introduce any special measures to stimulate economic development in the north. It could be argued that the development of the mineral resources of the country should be determined entirely by the current supply and demand position of the resources in question.
I am interrupting myself here in order to say that I have heard this argument presented in this House of Commons on several occasions.
If a zinc-lead deposit is found in a region which is so remote that it does not pay the mining company or the railroad company to build a railroad to the deposits, the normal contention would be that the deposits should be allowed to stay in the ground until other mines are used up and it becomes profitable to build a railroad. The same line of reasoning could be applied to the economic development of the north generally.
This line of argument might have considerable validity but for three facts. The first is that it is exploration as well as production which requires the stimulus of adequate transportation facilities. The second is that there is often a gap of between five and ten years between the time when a promising mineral deposit is discovered and when a mine can be brought fully into production-and in the north it is usually closer to ten years than five. This means that it is desirable to stimulate exploration approximately ten years


ahead of the time when it is believed that the production from a region will be required. If nothing is done until the demand exceeds the known supplies, then additional supplies in the remote area will not have been discovered and will not be ready to come into production. Consequently, for a period of five or ten years prices of certain vital raw materials will be substantially higher than would have been necessary if a more far-sighted policy had been adopted.
Then it goes on to give the reasons, that is to say the needs of the people who live in the north. Then this brief to the royal commission recommended three things that should be done in opening up the north. The first of these was a railroad to Great Slave lake. The second was development roads, not roads to known developments but roads to open up virgin resources in new areas. The third was air routes to the Arctic.
Mr. Chairman, I mention these three practical suggestions put forward by the commissioner of the Northwest Territories as evidence that there was knowledge in the ranks of officials of the federal government of what had to be done. But what was the attitude of the government in power? This report was never submitted to cabinet. There was no action taken on these recommendations made by this commissioner. It was left to the new government coming to power in 1957 to pick up this report ignored by the previous administration and take the necessary steps.
I would like to make it abundantly clear that when we speak of these development roads and I hear members of the official opposition standing up and saying that this submission was given to the Gordon commission when they were in power and that all these are their ideas, nothing could be further from the truth. Because a year after this submission was being transmitted to the Gordon commission we had a minister of the crown in that government, the former minister of northern affairs and national resources, speaking in Toronto at the meeting of the Empire club, on December 13, 1956.
I will not go through the whole 18 pages of his speech, but I would just read his conclusions. In his speech he described the list of things which the federal government was doing by itself and the list of things the federal government was doing in co-operation with the provinces. Then he pointed out that these resources belong to the provinces and that there is not very much the federal government can do. Then this is what he said about our national development plan, and I quote now from his speech:
To go beyond that, however, to try to impose an over-all blueprint, a national policy as some understand it, for resource management, to do that is to depart from the facts of our national situation. I have suggested already why such a master plan must fail in its purpose. In a country

as vast as Canada with widely different conditions and with different problems in different areas, there cannot be a single and unified policy for the management of resources.
Mr. Chairman, I have put this on the record before. Mr. Lesage's attitude was that you could not call a conservation conference, that the difficulties were so great and the regional problems so intricate that it would be impossible to get anything done. Therefore the government of that day continued a characteristic which had become part and parcel of them in the last ten years of their office. They were passive. They did nothing. They let these problems mount up and mount up and mount up and did nothing.
Mr. Chairman, that is why I used the expression in my opening remarks that this government differed from the previous administration; that we were a dynamic government; that we believed that private enterprise should develop our resources. We believed there were certain things which governments could do which would encourage private enterprise to go into the remote areas of our country and develop these resources for Canadians and by Canadians.
The Leader of the Opposition was somewhat concerned when I mentioned this and saw fit to get up and say that his party were dynamic. He quoted a speech of his in 1953 which listed all those things which should be done. All I point out is that if you want to say that some believe in declamations and not developments, there was that government. They made the declamation in 1953. There were officials of the government who made the representations to the Gordon commission, but the government did not take those recommendations seriously and did nothing about them.
I would like to point out by contrast just what this government did. Communications have been mentioned; I and other hon. members, including the hon. member for Mackenzie River, have said that communications in the north are vital. At the present time there is telephone communication-in fact at this very moment-between Ottawa and Frobisher bay; it went into effect last December. At the present time there are communication lines being built through Alberta, British Columbia, Yukon, right through to Alaska. At the present time there are communication lines being built leading up to Yellowknife; I think the target date for completion of the last two I have mentioned is next year. We have demonstrated, not by speeches made in 1953-

speechtext:
In spite of the fine speeches of the Leader of the Opposition in 1953, we have the speech of the responsible minister saying that nothing should be done.
Let me now pass on to the next thing we have done. It was clearly evident that there should be more knowledge of the north, one of the great valuable areas of the world lying unpopulated and uncontrolled. Outside of a few meteorologists, a few mounted policemen, a few Eskimos and a few odds and ends of government personnel from various sources, there was no one in these Arctic islands. We set up a polar continental shelf study under the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys, and now leading scientists of the government service are finding out these necessary things about our Arctic islands; they are providing the knowledge about and sovereignty over our country and helping private enterprise industries to go up there and find resources.
As to oceanography, there is an institute of oceanography being set up now in Halifax. Why was this not done years ago? To move into our northern islands in order to fully develop our shores we have to know about ocean currents. The Russians are leading the world in this work at the present time, and we are finally doing the things which should have been done a generation ago.
Then last year we spoke a little bit on the estimates about airfields. I would like to read a list of airfields built by this present government to help mining operations in the north. There is the airfield at Yellowknife mines; the airfield to be built at Rayrock mines in the Northwest Territories. There is the airfield we are still building for Taur-canis Mines Limited; and now there is a proposal before the government to build an airfield for Canada Tungsten Limited at Flat lake, Northwest Territories. I mention these things in communications and Arctic research to show we are moving forward.
With regard to the depths of our waters off our coasts, I asked the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys when we first came into office how long it would take, at the rate we were going, to get information about the depths of our channels and harbours in these northern areas and on our coasts, and the answer was 250 years. I maintain that a government that can move at that pace is not dynamic; it is as passive as a piece of jelly. It just jiggles and does not go any place.

Supply-Northern Affairs
I would like at this time to list the development roads we have built under the recommendation of this submission to the royal commission. There are the Yukon, Pelly and Stewart rivers which now have bridges across them which were not there two years ago. This makes it possible to double and triple the tonnage coming out of the mines in question there. We have rebuilt the Canol road up to the Ross river, and one of the most interesting discoveries in Canada is taking place there, the discovery of molybdenum which is used in hardening steel. Then there is the road from Watson Lake to Carmacks; construction was started this year. There is the road from Eagle plain which I have already described, and that was a road so vital to the oil industry that when we did not get through the pass which we had to overcome in the first 50 miles last year, the oil company was not even willing to wait until this year to do its exploration and built a temporary road 300 miles round the mountains so they could do their exploration last year.
Mr. Chairman, I mention these things in passing. I did not mention the road around Slave lake because it is under survey this year. I mentioned that our interest had been switched to the Fort Simpson-Laird-Fort Nelson road. I just list these things. We did not talk about what the royal commission recommended, nor did we make declamations about it. We took action, and that illustrates the difference between the passivity of the previous administration and the dynamic activity of the present government.
We know there is much to be done. We see these great sources of hydro power on the Yukon river. We see them in the east on the Hamilton river in Labrador. We know that before this country can move forward to the point where cheap processing of our goods is possible, we have to be able to harness and move tremendous reserves of energy from surplus to deficit areas.
The Prime Minister put this on record last September in the town of Kitimat, British Columbia. He indicated that what this country needs is a national power policy. This national power policy has as its heart and centre a grid tying together these great reserves of power in the remote areas in our north into which large quantities of surplus energy in electrical form can be poured at any time and taken off at any point.
This government did not just talk about this matter. It set up a special research group on long range transmission. I call as witness
[Mr. Hamilton (Qu'Appelle) .1
to this action the premier of British Columbia. Mr. Bennett knows about this and approves. He is quite interested in the Peace river and in having the northern part of his province hooked into this national grid. I call as witness the premier of Newfoundland. He has been made aware of our thinking in this regard and has spoken of it highly. In fact I think he got carried away with enthusiasm one night at a service club dinner and divulged what was going on with respect to the possibility of some people from Russia coming in. I call as witness, too, the previous administration of the province of Quebec, as well as a representative of Ontario hydro, Mr. Hearn, the president, Mr. Duncan, and Mr. Cass-Beggs of the Saskatchewan power commission.
