I suggest too, Mr. Chairman, that a country with the great resources we have of butane, propane and other L.P.G. fuels which are going to waste in many parts of the country must bring these into deficit areas. If this were done our whole country would be better off.
The hon. member for Laurier asked about the Pine Point railway. I think it is time I put before the committee some of the facts about this matter. The Pine Point railway was recommended in the submission of the commissioner of the Northwest Territories in 1955, and the previous government did nothing about it. In 1958 there was mention of it in the speech from the throne. We were willing as a government to go ahead and build that railway, because we knew first of all from the over-all position of the lead and zinc supplies of the world that there was

need to get moving fast in the production of more lead and zinc in Canada. At that time we knew there was a surplus, but we also knew it would take several years to bring this mine into operation.
We put ourselves on record as being willing to build this railway. However, the local people in Alberta, by representations to the government and by statements in the press, indicated that there was a difference of opinion as to where this railway should be built. We had cognizance of the fact that in a democracy where there are differences of opinion, those differences should be brought before a body who could reach some determination. The governments of British Columbia, Saskatchewan and Alberta and the people of those provinces as well as various companies made representations on the subject. The report is now before the government.
I am not going to make any comments on the report itself with but two exceptions. The decision of the members of the commission is clear to all those who have read the report. I think certain facts should be brought forward. In the first place this railway is estimated to cost over $65 million. The government will have to put up not $65 million or $68 million-whatever it comes to, we do not know-but the traditional subsidy to development railways which is $25,000 per mile, or roughly $10 million, and the railway companies will have to put up the balance. That is one fact.
The second thing on which I should like to comment is this. The suggestion was made in the report of the royal commission that it might be possible to take this tonnage out by road from the Pine Point mine. Theoretically that is possible, but I want to warn hon. members of the committee that the report ignores the question of who is going to build and who is going to pay for the road to bring out this 200,000 tons of ore a year. In the opinion of my engineering officials the capital cost of building a gravel road would be in the neighbourhood of $39 million, and the capital cost of a paved road would be $53 million. The cost of the operation and paying capital expenditures indicates that once you reach the figure of approximately 95,000 tons per year it would be cheaper to build the railroad than to construct a road. If the road were paved and the cost were higher it would take a higher tonnage before it was balanced off; or in plain terms, the cost of building and maintaining a road for a tonnage greater than roughly 100,000 tons a year is such that it would be better in the long run to build a railway.
Supply-Northern Affairs
I mention that because with these facts in mind, in view of the government's willingness to go ahead with this railroad, it is clearly evident where the government stands on what it wants to do. I have not had much help from the commission in deciding on the route.
Let me deal with another point under this heading. I was asked by the Leader of the Opposition if we considered markets when we went into these development projects. The implication was that if you did not consider the marketing possibilities there was no use opening up the mine. It is no longer a secret that if this mine is not in production by 1963 or 1964, lead and zinc will have to be imported into Canada to keep the smelters going at Trail. Those things were in the mind of my department when we made the proposition to the government that this railroad should be built. It is true that world lead and zinc prices had gone down at that time. It is true that there was an embargo or quota system against lead and zinc going into the United States. It is also true, however, that we proceeded in spite of these things, because we believed that the United States had no right to look upon us as an extension of their economy.
As minister of Canadian resources it was my responsibility and duty to recommend those things that would keep Canada in a position wherein our great reserves of lead and zinc in this country could be utilized and we would not be forced into the position of having to import. The extent of the importation can be realized by the following figures which I wish to place on the record concerning average foreign purchases.

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: Before the minister proceeds perhaps he will permit me to ask a question. If parliament were to approve the building of the Pine Point railway at its 1961 session how long, according to the information available to the minister, would it take to build the railway and have it ready for operation?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: In that case it would not estop the importation of lead and zinc from other countries?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: That is quite true, Mr. Chairman. What I am trying to do is build up the evidence that assists people to realize the importance of going ahead with this railway.

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
May I ask the minister a question? Is there any disposition, as seen

Supply-Northern Affairs by the minister, on the part of the Alberta government to participate in the capital cost of the railway?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
The MacGregor royal commission report on northern Alberta recommended that the government of Alberta participate in the cost of the bridge going across the Peace river, but I have not had any communication from the Alberta government showing its willingness to participate.
May I now give the figures to which I referred. It is estimated that the cost of imports at the Trail plant would be $14 million; it is estimated that in addition we would lose exports valued at $7 million a year, or there would be a total change in our foreign exchange balance of $21 million a year, owing to this railway not being built.
I have put the facts before the committee, Mr. Chairman, with the idea of giving some basis for an objective conclusion on the part of the people of Canada in making up their minds about what should be done with respect to the Pine Point railway.
I have transgressed on the time of the committee, Mr. Chairman, so I am going to conclude with this statement and I shall make it as strong as I can. The purpose of the government in its national development policy is to have more processing in Canada. This processing in Canada cannot come from sitting here idly, passively and letting things work out by themselves. We believe that in today's economics and today's world competition what is required is to get down to the simple basic facts of producing something cheaper than any other nation can produce it. This means that where you have great resources of energy in juxtaposition with great resources of natural products, and where these can be brought together to produce something cheaper by uniting the energy with the resources, we can hold our own in the world competition battle as a processing country.
Second, we believe that with the Canadian ingenuity, so well demonstrated in the past, in the field of metallurgy, our scientists will produce new types of steel, steel mixed with uranium, steel mixed with molybdenum, steel hardened with titanium, steels that can stand cold weather, steels that will meet competition all over the world; and by keeping ahead in the metallurgical field we can move into foreign markets and retain our position in our own markets.
Also we do believe that there has to be a great deal of co-operation between the federal government and the provinces in working with our resources as a whole, and not 11 different government agencies all going


their own way and all losing out in this battle that we are in. Whether it affects the Combines Investigation Act, which allows industries to share market information or to combine on research or to come together on export products; whether it is a question of the scientific work of governments or industry, these are things that must all be tied up under the over-all watchfulness of 11 governments which own these resources, and that is one of the main reasons why we have set up this conservation conference to meet next year.
No, Mr. Chairman; the vision that we talk about as a government does have enthusiasm, but it is no mirage. It does have idealism, but we do the things that are practical and realistic. It is a vision which to us is logical and coherent in so far as development is concerned. It does take in all the facts of life there are in Canada in relation to these resources. Let me put it as simply as I can. Canadians all working together can achieve the things that we have in mind.
I think I should point out that the program I have described is a national development program only in the first stages. The second, third and fourth stages are still to come, but much has to be done before we even reach those stages. I am very glad of the opportunity the committee has given me to meet head on the statements of the members of the opposition on this question of the national development policy of the government. It gives me a chance to put forward very clearly the distinctions between us. I think the debate has been carried on on a very high level; I think it has done a great deal of good to clear the minds of many hon. members and I do trust of the people of the country as a whole.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: May I ask the minister a question now that he has completed his remarks? speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am not trained in the dialectics of certain people, and all I can say in answer to the observation of the hon. member for Laurier is that I think the people will measure us by results and not by the words we use.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: May I say it was not a dialect I was using but the other official language of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: Still dialectic.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I wonder
whether the Leader of the Opposition would permit me to ask a question. In view of the protests of the people of Alberta, would he have built the railway without giving them a chance to put forward their viewpoint?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I should like to ask the minister why they said in the election campaigns of 1957 and 1958 that they would do it at once. Why did he not think about this consideration then? Why did the government put in their very first speech from the throne that they would appropriate money for the building of the railroad in 1958? Why did they not think about this other factor at that time? Now he tells us they had to take a lot of time to get the views of the people, and in order to do so they had to set up a royal commission, all of which takes time. Of course it does. But when we point out to him that it took time when we were in office he says that we were passive and did not do anything. Again there is a contrast between the words of the minister and the facts.
Although not strictly relevant to this item, the minister talked this afternoon about roads to resources, development roads. When I was talking the other day I mentioned one particular road which would be a road to a resource and which would assist in the salvation of the community at Elliot Lake. He had never heard of it. The provincial government of Ontario had heard about it, his colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce had heard about it, but the minister had never heard about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Order. I do not see
any question of privilege. It is just a disagreement.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: I accept the minister's remarks even though there is no question of privilege. He says he knew there was such a project but it had not been brought to his attention.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: I must rise again. If the Leader of the Opposition will examine the record, and I did not change it, he will And I said I had not been informed officially by the government of Ontario. I knew the committee had been discussing that road, but I had not been approached officially.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
All right; the minister has not been informed officially about this particular road to resources which had been announced officially by the province of Ontario as something that was going to be done and about which they had been in conversation and conference with the federal government. The minister had better consult his colleague and his friends in Toronto. He says he had not been told about it officially, but his government apparently has, because they seem to know something about it.
I mention this matter once again to pour the cold water of reality on the minister's exuberant statements. The other day and again this afternoon the minister seemed to take a great deal of pleasure in deprecating the record of his predecessor, Mr. Lesage, a record which will stand on its own and does not need any apology from us on this side. As found on page 6869 of Hansard of last Saturday, the minister was trying to point out that nothing had been done by the previous government. He said that he held the previous administration responsible for not looking after those very valuable resources in the north country. He repeated this afternoon that nothing had been done until 1957 and that we were responsible, especially Mr. Lesage, for the fact that the resources of our north country had not been looked after.
He criticized Mr. Lesage particularly because apparently at one stage he had made a statement in Toronto in which he pointed out and underlined the difficulties of management of our resources in this country except in full co-operation with the provinces, he quite rightly pointed out that the federal government has not control of and cannot plan or manage resources except in co-operation with the provinces, which is a very sound and sensible doctrine, the only doctrine under which we can develop our resources in Canada.
I am going to quote some of the statements the minister made on Saturday, because I cannot be contradicted when I read from Hansard. My memory of what the minister said this afternoon might not be accurate in every respect, because the minister proceeded very quickly and eloquently
[The Deputy Chairman.]
and it was hard to follow his words; but in talking about the development of the north he did say on Saturday, as found on page 6869 of Hansard:
The real task was to make certain that the oil, gas and mineral wealth of our northern areas, particularly those in the Arctic islands, would be preserved for Canadians-
"Would be preserved".
[DOT]-now and in the future.
He also had this to say about the oil, gas and mining regulations which have been put into effect in recent months, which show how this wealth is going to be preserved for Canadians now and in the future. He was referring to the regulations, the exploration permits which were given and the methods that were adopted to attract foreign capital, which he thinks can be so damaging to us, and as found on page 6870 he said:
In other words, we gave a cheap land proposition to the oil industry of the world-
Presumably that is how the minister is going to preserve-that was the word he used-for Canadians the resources of the north by giving a cheap land proposition to the oil industry of the world. He also made this statement, as found on page 6869, as another illustration of the virtuous endeavours of the government in this field of development of resources:
Naturally when we began to work out these new regulations we began to think in terms of how we can stop, how we can prevent what has happened in Alberta...
In other words-perhaps the minister will explain this-what they were thinking about, among other things, was how they could prevent federally what has happened in Alberta in this industry. On the subject of preserving for Canada control of its resources, there is no difference of opinion between members of the house as to the desirability of ensuring maximum Canadian participation and maximum Canadian control in the development, management and ownership of these resources. We are all agreed on that, but some of us know more than the minister seems to know about the difficulties of reconciling the necessity of foreign investment and the primary necessity of Canadian control of our own resources.
As found on page 6871 of Hansard the minister talked about the yoke-that was the word he used-of foreign capital, the yoke of foreign investment, and the great progress that had been made in Canada under the present government in freeing Canada from that yoke of foreign investment. There has been a great deal of progress, I admit, in talking about that freedom and that yoke, but what do the figures show as to the progress that has been made in freeing

Canada from what the minister called the yoke of foreign investment? Referring to the dominion bureau of statistics "Balance of International Payments 1959", page 14, and the "Canadian Balance of International Payments, 1958", table 8. I am only going to quote one excerpt from these publications. They bear reading in relation to the boast the minister has made about the progress this government has made in freeing us from this yoke. These figures are from official publications; on the balance of international payments, from the part entitled "Non-resident ownership and control of Canadian industry".
The last detailed analysis of foreign ownership was issued in December of last year and covers the year 1957. The balance of payments officials have, however, made estimates of the total non-resident owned long term investment in Canada for the years 1958 and 1959. This series contains an estimate of retained earnings in Canada plus long term investment. It thus is a valid measure of the growth of foreign ownership in Canada.
Here are the figures: 1956, total non-resident investment in Canada amounted to $15.6 billion; 1957, $17.5 billion; 1958, $19.1 billion; 1959, $20.6 billion. The only conclusion that can be drawn from these figures is that total non-resident ownership has increased by one third since 1956. This is how we have been freed from the yoke of foreign investment. While the minister talked about the "yoke" his leader, the Prime Minister, referred to foreign investment in somewhat different terms. I quote from his statement which appears on page 6873 of Hansard for July 23, 1960:
Foreign investment is beneficial. Foreign investment has done much to improve the economical situation in Canada.
Then he went on to emphasize that external capital had played a very important part in our development. This is just another example, Mr. Chairman, of that schizophrenia that seems to afflict the members of the cabinet. The minister in his statement this afternoon repeated what the Prime Minister said; that the yoke, in so far as foreign investment in the United States was concerned, was never at any time more than 15 per cent of the national income. That was the figure the minister used, while the Prime Minister said that in Canada the corresponding proportion as late as 1957 was almost 75 per cent. Perhaps the minister will try to confirm this figure, that as late as 1957 the corresponding figure for foreign investment in Canada was 75 per cent of our national income. Obviously the Prime Minister was not very careful about his statistics on this matter.

Then the Prime Minister went on to say, and the minister confirmed it this afternoon, that this situation is improving. I have given the figures to show how the situation is improving. The total non-resident ownership has increased by one third since 1956. If the situation has improved however, in the sense that in the last 18 months less foreign capital has come into this country for development purposes, we know the reason for that. Perhaps the minister will get a lot of comfort out of the fact that there has been a decrease in foreign investment capital coming into this country lately. Perhaps he will be very pleased that this may be interpreted as freeing us from the yoke of foreign control. There is another reason to explain that decrease in foreign investment in the last 18 months, and that reason was given by the deputy chairman of the dollar-sterling trade council, writing in the Financial Post of May 21, 1960. I shall quote two paragraphs from this article by A. G. S. Griffin, deputy chairman of the dollar-sterling trade council. He said:
The past 18 months have seen an important change in the attitude of U.K. and foreign investors toward Canada.
Visitors to London and other European financial capitals can no longer bask in a glow of satisfaction from plaudit heaped upon plaudit over the way we run our country, treat our foreign capital and develop our resources.
There is a good deal of grumbling and some positive indignation-as if the overseas investor had been the victim of some vast conspiracy.
Then, Mr. Chairman, on Saturday the Prime Minister had something to say about his vision of the north. Perhaps I had better read what he said:
Mr. Chairman, a word on these vast potential resources. Somebody spoke of a mirage. Until the vision of the north turns out to be a mirage let me say that the millions and millions of acres which have been taken up in the north, the developments which have taken place there, the opening up of the country and the rendering available to private enterprise of an opportunity and a climate for development has meant much to Canada during the past three years.
I will ask the minister now to give us the figures in regard to this development in terms of oil and gas exploration permits, and also to give us the figures or give us the information regarding the nationality of the companies and corporations that are responsible for taking up these permits, whether they are United States corporations, whether they are Canadian subsidiaries of United States corporations, whether they are other foreign corporations or whether they are bona fide Canadian individuals and Canadian corporations.
The Prime Minister went on to say:
I remember speaking in 1957 and in 1958 about the highways in the north and the opening of the north igloo to igloo. That was the viewpoint of the opposition.

Supply-Northern Affairs
I will repeat what I said the other day, Mr. Chairman; that the program put forward by the Prime Minister and his colleagues during that election period was not a program of development, it was a program of electoral intoxication. When they talked about this great program of development, this great billion dollar public works program, this great program of communications and transportation which was going to solve the unemployment problem or play a large part in solving the unemployment problem, we on this side said that was a phony program in terms of employment. It has turned out to be just that.
The minister did not reply to me on Saturday when I asked him how much employment had been provided by road development in the north since he gave the last figures, which was something over 2,000 men for the previous year.

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: May I ask the Leader of the Opposition what he means by "north"? I want him to be specific.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I mean by "north" the areas under federal control, and those areas where the government has initiated a roads to resources program with the provinces; that is the kind of roadbuilding and communications program which was put forward by the government to cope with our unemployment problem.
Then the minister had this to say, as reported on page 6869 of Hansard for July 23, 1960. He talked about this great Canadian proposal which has won for Canada the control of the continental shelf. I will read what he had to say about it.
We have brought those regulations in, using the Public Lands Grants Act and the Territorial Lands Act, and for the first time in Canada's history we have the legal machinery to give to Canadians or to anybody else the right to explore in our Arctic Islands or in those islands off the coast. I hold the previous administration responsible through the error of omission for not looking after those very valuable resources north of our country.
Well, I have dealt with that. Then he went on to say that as the result of a Canadian resolution-no, I had better quote what he said about it:
It is no accident that the Canadian resolution on the law of the sea conference in Geneva suggested that all the lands that lie beneath the sea, the continental shelf, as far out as you can develop them, should belong to the littoral state for exploration purposes.
Well, I should like to have the minister tell this committee when that specific Canadian proposal was put before the international law conference at Geneva which established the jurisdiction of the littoral state over the continental shelf. If I am not wrong- and the minister can correct me if I am wrong

-the proposal appeared in the original report of the United Nations commission which was preparing for this conference. The minister now points out that it was the Canadian proposal that secured for Canada the continental shelf. What happened was that this was discussed at the conference at Geneva. There was general agreement on it, and as a result of that agreement all countries now have accepted and recognized control over the resources of the continental shelf. But when we asked the minister, as reported at page 6873 of Hansard of last Saturday, what was the relationship of this doctrine to provincial control-and this is an important matter, who actually controlled the continental shelf off provincial coasts as contrasted with the continental shelf off federal territories-who actually controlled the resources of that part of the shelf, the provincial government or the federal government, the minister said:
This is a matter of government policy and will be declared in due course.
My friend the hon. member for Ottawa East asked this question:
Has the minister had any requests from the provinces for the transfer of rights on the continental shelf?
The minister's reply was no, but the fact is this, as the minister must know. Indeed, in an earlier question-

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I wonder
whether the Leader of the Opposition would help me. I just want to understand clearly what he said. He stated that I said that the matter of the continental shelf ownership was a matter of government policy. Can he point out to me where I said that?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: I have said two things. The minister now claims that this great development in international law by which the state has control of the continental shelf was the result of a Canadian proposal at Geneva, and I asked for information about that matter. I have also said that the minister said that the question as to whether the crown in the right of the provinces or the crown in the right of the federal government controlled the resources on the continental shelf off provincial coasts is a matter of government policy which will be announced in due course.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: From where does that quotation come? I never made that statement.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
If the minister will just read his own words in Hansard of last Saturday as reported at page 6873, and that is not very far back, he will find that in answer to a

question asked by my friend the hon. member for Villeneuve, to be found down toward the end of the page, he replied as follows:
This is a matter of government policy and will be declared in due course.
He also said earlier, according to press reports, when he was questioned about the matter of ownership of the continental shelf by the federal or provincial authority, "So far we have not stirred anybody up on this". But this is a matter which has already been stirred up in the provinces. At the Atlantic provinces conference last September, held in Fredericton, the premier of Nova Scotia at that time-that was last September-called, for a decision on the ownership of submarine mineral rights. I am now quoting from press accounts of the meeting:
Premier Stanfield also called for a decision on the ownership of submarine mineral rights. He said the constitutional question of whether they belonged to the province or to the government of Canada should be settled.
Indeed it should be settled, because it is one of the most important questions that can face the federation at the present time; that is to say, who owns those rights on the continental shelf. The minister says, however, it is a matter of policy and "we are not stirring anybody up about this".
There are many other things I could say and there are many other questions that we shall be asking because of what the minister has already said. But I think I have put on the record sufficient to indicate the situation. In spite of the eloquence of the minister and in spite of the exuberance of words that came from him this afternoon and on Saturday, the record itself will determine, as the minister says, the result that will be achieved. And when he talks about the passive record of the Liberal government in the past I ask him to look at the record from 1900 to 1910, from 1920 to 1931 and from 1945 to 1957. If he thinks that Canada developed in those great years of development through passive governments he had better read a little bit more of his history than he has been reading lately. In conclusion I remind the minister once again that no matter what he may say, history in this country did not begin in June of 1957.

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
As the third history teacher speaking in this debate, I should like to get into it and say that I should like to make some historical comments also. I was flabbergasted last Saturday when, in the quiet of this committee, with perhaps 30 or 35 members present, who should rise and take part in the debate but the Prime Minister. Here on the eve of a dominion-provincial conference he found the time to come in and give us his reinterpretation of the vision.
Supply-Northern Affairs This procedure seemed to me to underline the importance that he and the minister must attach to the vision for some purposes which I hope to analyse.
I thought at first that this was a bit of an insult to the minister. It is a rare occasion when a prime minister comes in and defends in essence the general position of a department in the government frame of policy when the minister is before the house. But I do not see the matter in quite that way now. I see it more in terms of an abnormal sensitivity on the part of the Prime Minister and the government with regard to the most blatant or, one could put it, the most flagrant of their political promises and their inability to live up to it.
I should like to ask the minister whether he has ever stopped to wonder why it was that in northern Ontario, from the Manitoba border all the way down to south of Sudbury, the Conservative party in this last election, which he said gave them carte blanche, or words to that effect, or at least a criticism of the Liberal party's position toward the north-did so badly in that part of the country. I should like to tell him one of the reasons is that the people of northern and northwestern Ontario live in an area where we have, to use this phrase that is so overused, vast, boundless natural resources, loads of them. They are much closer to markets and to people in this country than are the resources of the north.
I cannot think of a bigger laugh than that which was caused in our particular region during that election campaign when the minister, I think, or perhaps it was the Prime Minister, came up with the story of how they were going to build a road from somewhere up near Hudson bay down toward lake Superior. It was almost as ridiculous as this suggestion that they are negotiating with the Ontario government to build a road north somewhere between Nakina and the Manitoba boundary, over 400 miles of space.
The people of northwestern and northern Ontario were sceptical of this suggestion on practical grounds. They know that within their region they have copper prospects, zinc prospects, iron ore prospects, gold prospects and all sorts of forest resources that are still not being used. They know they still have certain water power resources. They know they have natural gas moving through there in a pipe line so that it can be used for various developments. They also know that their resources which are being exploited at the present time in the main are being exploited by United States capital and United States corporations.

Supply-Northern Affairs
Hence they are sceptical of the northern vision on two counts. Why not a bit of concentration upon an area that is closer to markets and closer to where there is a labour force that is in trouble? Second, the taint that this particular government in electioneering put upon United States capital does not make much sense to people in an area which for most of its industry depends upon United States capital. This phase of the Prime Minister's electoral activity of trying to batten upon the almost natural instinct of the people to distrust United States efforts it seems to me has gone far enough. It seems to me that the Prime Minister himself has spoiled it by his inability really to do anything about it.
I note that in his speech on Saturday he mentioned going down to the city of Detroit and laying some things on the line. I can remember that Right Hon. C. D. Howe went down to Chicago, to Milwaukee and to Washington, and that he laid some things on the line; but it did not seem to do very much good. It did just about as much good as what the Prime Minister has done. I would suggest to the minister that he throw away this word "vision". Let us have a fairly cool policy of northern development and stop all the extravagant claims about what Canada is going to get out of the north.
In his remarks just after lunch the minister indicated that while this government would never interfere with provincial jurisdiction, these new mining regulations would be a bellwether to the provinces, that the people of the provinces would demand legislation just like it. I know that school teachers- the minister was one and so was I-tend to be naive, but I refuse to believe the minister is that naive and that he really thinks these regulations will be a bellwether to the provinces and will lead the people in the provinces to demand from their governments the kind of redress which one can find, say, in the iron ore contracts in Newfoundland and Labrador.
I do not know why Duplessis and Smallwood sold out to these companies in the way they did for so little by way of fee; but to suggest that we will get any kind of redress through a few regulations is beyond me, and I cannot understand how the suggestion can be made. If the minister is going to say at his conservation conferences that this government would project a policy on the development of Canadian resources in the provinces or in the Canadian north in the highest possible finished state, then I can see that he would be making a contribution; otherwise this is just a continuation of the sham stuff we had in the last election, and which


I repeat northwestern Ontario did not buy; and they sure are not going to buy it next time either.
The Prime Minister in his remarks touched on what this country had done to really put Americans in their place; at least I interpreted it in that way. He said something about insurance companies and he said something about oil. Oil certainly is not a minor factor, and I suppose insurance companies are not. But if you are going to do something about United States investment, and this government feels that something should be done, why does it not begin with iron ore? Across the country from contacts I have had with ordinary people I hear time and again, why can we not process iron ore in this country?
The minister has economists who turn out reports. There have been several in the last year right on this very question. What do the reports say? That the economics of the situation are such that we cannot look forward to any great expansion in the treatment of iron ores in Canada other than perhaps in a minor way so far as beneficiation is concerned. The most recent report on the direct reduction process indicated that there might be an economic feasibility of having such a development at Port Arthur and Seven Islands. However, in the main the great bulk of our ore will continue to go down in a raw or semi-raw state to United States smelters.
If this government feels so strongly and wants to give leadership to this blatant antiAmerican feeling that there is in Canada, how about doing something about the iron ore situation? The sound and fury we have heard in connection with what the government is going to do in the north is to me about the worst kind of nonsense that this government has come up with.
I suggest to the minister that in population terms the north is really not growing, except in civil servants who are being sent up there. I would ask, in investment terms what is being turned out in the north? Is it possible that in the north, in the sense of the northwest, are we really going to get any forestry production which will enter the markets of the world or even the markets of southern Canada? How many tons of iron ore are being shipped from the domains which are under the minister? How many barrels of oil are being shipped? How much is being shipped in the way of base metals? I think that is about the only area where the minister will find he has any production, and it is not very large.
Mr. Chairman, one could spend much more time than I have and the Leader of the Opposition has spent on this question of the

vision. I want to make the point that in my remarks I am not supporting the great defence he has made with regard to activity in the past. It seems to me that this government has the intention of doing better than the Liberal government did in pushing the greater use and manufacture of Canadian resources in Canada, but I certainly cannot see that they have attained any success in this field. All they have done is make a great deal of propaganda, and make the very word "vision" in political terms a joke across the country.
Now I would like to turn to something a little more specific, and that is the statement which was apparently made by the hon. member for Yukon either on June 1 or May 31. I cannot find any record of it in the House of Commons debates, but he is on record as having said, according to a Globe and Mail story by reporter Walter Gray:
A bureaucratic regime is operating in the office of the commissioner of the Yukon territory, the territorial member of parliament charged here today.
Eric Nielsen (PC, Yukon), added quickly that he was not criticizing the incumbent commissioner, F. H. Collins, but the office itself. He blamed the five-man territorial council for failing to assume more executive responsibility in an effort to correct the situation which has built up over the years.
The young member noted that of 112 ordinances consolidated by territorial council in 1958, 71 gave extraordinary powers to the commissioner who is able to issue regulations without reference to council.
"These powers have not been abused so far, but the ease with which they could be abused is frightening", said Mr. Nielsen in an interview.
He went on to give a more detailed criticism, and then said:
"The council should be encouraged to take on more executive responsibility," he said. "There must be a feeling in the commissioner to relieve himself of administrative powers to assist in the democratic development of the Yukon. I'm afraid there is a reluctance on the part of the administration to divest itself of these powers."
Mr. Chairman, we cannot get into the private circles of the government in power, but we would not have expected that the hon. member for Yukon would have had such difficulty. I understood that he had practically a free run of the bureaux at the department of northern affairs, and that he spent more time there than he did anywhere else; yet after almost three sessions at the job, what could he come up with except criticism of this northern administration?
Mr. Chairman, I think we deserve a satisfactory answer, not from the hon. member for Yukon but from the minister. How can he explain that a member of his own party, to whom he has given a great deal of credit
Supply-Northern Affairs for his interest, can come out into the open with criticism like this and not expect us to want an answer?
It would be foolish for us to assume that we know anything about the northern administration in relation to what the hon. member on the scene must know. I would say the hon. member for Yukon, according to this account in the Globe and Mail, has been exceptionally critical. I wonder why he has not been put into the same category as the hon. member for Restigouche-Mada-waska, because this is real criticism. When you consider that he has had three sessions to go to work on this to get some kind of redress, is this an indication that the minister has no control over his own civil servants?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:

The hon. member for Port Arthur should

Those criticisms of the hon. member for the Yukon were directed against the local government in that area and not against my civil servants at all.

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: As I understand it, the minister has something to do with the incumbent commissioners.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
My job is to
appoint them. I have nothing whatever to do with the decisions of the territorial council either in the Northwest Territories or the Yukon.

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: What role does the northern administration play in the Yukon territories? Does this not come up under the northern administration branch?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: The explanation, Mr. Chairman, is that we look after resources in the territories and also some aspects of Eskimo welfare and education and Indian welfare and education.

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
In this article I notice that Mr. Gray states that the commissioner, with a salary this year of $10,500, is appointed at the pleasure of the governor in council. When we are talking about other government appointees of the governor in council I always thought this meant that the governor in

Supply-Northern Affairs council had some kind of control over the appointees. Is the minister suggesting that Mr. Collins operates in limbo without any departmental or cabinet control?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: That is precisely what I am saying, Mr. Chairman, that the federal government appoints the commissioner but exercises no control whatever over matters under territorial jurisdiction. The practice has been growing up of permitting an increasing autonomy in the area. I am trying to encourage that in every way. I would not think of interfering in a matter between the territorial government and one of its citizens.

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: To what audience does the hon. member for the Yukon address himself? Did the minister tell the hon. member that this was something in which he did not take an interest because he feels the federal government should not interfere in any way with the council there?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: This is not under my jurisdiction but I understand the hon. member spoke to the board of trade in Whitehorse on their invitation purely as a citizen of the Yukon. It does not come under my responsibility. In fact, I would fight very hard to protect the rights of the territorial government to look after its own business.

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:

Was he talking to the local people or did he have in mind the deputy minister of northern affairs who has something to do with the board that produces these ordinances. The hon. gentleman is quoted as going on to say that the council should take on more executive responsibility. Is he talking to the council or to the government?

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.

speechtext: I have to be fair. All throughout this matter the hon. member for the Yukon has shown a keen interest. There were discussions last year between the hon. gentleman and myself about strengthening the council. Also the council met last year in formal session and passed a resolution-not an ordinance-suggesting that this change be made. I asked the House of Commons to make that change and it did.

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: I am still bothered by this question of the man appointed being outside the orbit of departmental control.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order. Since this discussion commenced the hon. member for Port Arthur has been making reference to the hon. member for the Yukon with whom I have the honour to share an office. The hon. member for Port Arthur suggested that the hon. member for the Yukon spends most of his time over at the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources. I would say to the hon. gentleman that if he worked half as hard as does the hon. member for the Yukon he would be considerably better informed and would not engage in nonsensical allegations.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: Order. The remarks of the hon. member are argumentative. If the hon. gentleman wishes to rise after the hon. member for Port Arthur has concluded he may do so, but he is not allowed to interrupt the hon. member for that purpose.

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
The hon. member has made a wrong interpretation of my remarks. I did not intend to reflect on the work done by the hon. member for the Yukon. I admire him very much for getting up and saying this kind of thing. What I meant by his being over at the department was this. I served on the committee with him last year. It was obvious that he knew everyone there. The hon. gentleman told me he spent a great deal of time

with the department and I have heard others say he does. If there are matters affecting him he should spend as much time as possible pressuring civil servants. I am merely trying to find out if he has been making any headway. My remarks were not intended to be derogatory or insulting to the hon. member for the Yukon.
Perhaps the minister could explain in greater detail how he reconciles the fact that he and the Prime Minister speak of the north as a great area where the federal government is showing leadership and yet the representative from the area makes a criticism which seems to indicate that the great vision is blurred in at least one of the most important fundamental areas involving the democratic control of the affairs of the area by the citizens who live there under this bureaucratic regime.
The minister has often talked about the road to resources program. I raised this matter with him last week in connection with the access to roads where the government makes a contribution. The hon. gentleman gave me the flat assurance which I accepted that wherever the federal government makes a contribution to the roads to resources program and no matter what contribution the company may make the road is open and free of access to everyone.
Perhaps the minister is aware that we have an example in our constituency. The road runs for some 60 miles. The two governments and the company made a contribution. Sixty miles of the road is open but in the middle of the wilderness the road comes to a gate on the edge of the company's property. There is a further stretch of six miles of road that leads to where activities are actually going on. There is public access to the first 60 miles but no one can get through the gates to travel the last six miles unless the company wants them to. I hope the minister will give an assurance that in future agreements that may be made under this section of the act care will be taken to see that this kind of situation is not repeated.
I can underline this by pointing out that this United States corporation has set up what we call a company union and is involved in certification proceedings at this very moment. It uses that gate to keep union organizers out. I do not know whether they are also using it to keep out salesmen or other entrepreneurs who want to get in; but in effect this government has supported, through funds, a 60-mile road that leads to nowhere in so far as the public is concerned. I have to assume that a vacuum cleaner salesman or a union organizer has just as much right to go to the end of a road that the government helps pay for as 79951-0-446
Supply-Northern Affairs anyone else, and yet this road ends at a gate in the bush. No one can go past it. I should like an assurance from the minister that in future in connection with roads to resources we shall not have roads which in effect end nowhere. If these roads lead to resources development, then the public should have access to that development. I do not see why the minister cannot make that part of the agreements in the future. Take as an example Anaconda. The minister has a good argument with the provincial government and any firm which may be involved in a matter of this kind. I should very much like to have his comments on this particular story.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: In regard to the road to the Anaconda property, I informed the committee on Saturday that in so far as any road in which we share the costs with a province and a company is concerned, there certainly is public access. It poses a very difficult problem for me. If any company builds up to that access road a private road of its own and pays 100 per cent of the cost of it, do I have to insist that a road connecting on to our road shall have public access? I do not think I can give that assurance, frankly, because first of all it does not lie within the jurisdiction of the federal government to insist on what shall be done in a province. Second, I think it would be an interference with the rights of private ownership. If I am a private owner in that area and I build a road up to a road built by the federal government and the province in co-operation, have I not a right to maintain my private property? I think we would be interfering with the rights of private property. I am putting the argument forward. I realize what the hon. member has in mind, but I do not think I can go beyond saying that the roads that we have already built are free access roads. That is as far as I can go.

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
The minister may be aware of the mining laws and claims in that area. The Anaconda interest can stretch for some 20 or 30 miles, and other properties go even farther. We can see where we have a virtual private empire of a United States corporation up in northern Ontario. The government of Ontario has committed itself to putting the road in there, and yet the company can determine everything that takes place in that big empire. I will admit that there may be some limits on what this government may be able to argue other than the lever it has through its contribution.
Surely the provincial government which issues the licences for these huge territories that come under the sway of such men should

Supply-Northern Affairs be prepared to listen to suggestions from the minister. I cannot help but feel that the minister and the department are letting themselves into an almost indefensible position from the public point of view. If the minister wants to look at the general unpopularity that the pulp and paper companies have managed to maintain by keeping their roads closed on much greater justification than this, I think he will see what I mean. There is a potential here for one of the sharpest issues that have ever come up in our part of the country.
I just suggest to the minister that in writing any new agreements he does more to see that such a thing does not happen again. If Anaconda actually had an open pit or a shaft, or something like that, going on in there I could certainly see every reason why they should have the right to protect that property from access by outsiders, but when you are going to have what is in effect a town developing in there a townsite, and you are able to put up a gate and keep everybody out of that area because you control the gate at the end of the road toward which the government contributed I think it is going too far. I think a narrower distinction may be made. I suggest to the minister he should try to make it.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: I should like to give the hon. member for Port Arthur the assurance that I shall certainly keep that in mind. I should like to say that we impress on any government that makes this arrangement with us that as far as we are concerned these are public access roads and we are not a party to practices such as have been described here. But legally I do not think I have the power to change any agreement already made. I will certainly give the assurance that in the future I shall make it very plain that these are public roads. I have already done so but I will do so again.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am tempted to rise at this point and take issue with some of the things that were said by the minister on Saturday and again this afternoon as well as with what was said by the Prime Minister on Saturday prior to the opening of the dominion-provincial conference. I am surprised that in his remarks the minister would have been so pronounced in the general statement that when he took office little or nothing had been done by the previous administration and that everything that has been done, has been accomplished since he and those associated with him have been in office.
I should like to remind the minister-I cannot remember the date now but certainly it would be around 1950-that when I occupied a position on the other side of

the house similar to his I made a trip over the northwest passage and to airports that had been built by the previous government and not by this government. He had a great deal to say about airstrips that had been built and roads and a future railway. The trip that was made by my officers and myself, was by way of Edmonton to Fort Smith.

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: Get to the point.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I am getting to the point, and the point I am getting to is that before this government came into office in 1957 a great deal more had been accomplished by the previous administration than the minister would like us to believe. One of the first things that was done was the establishment of the department over which the minister presides now. This department was established by the previous administration. It was taken out of the department of resources and development and made a department by itself, namely the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources at the head of which at one time, if not at the beginning, was the present premier of the province of Quebec. I deprecate the statement which the present minister made on Saturday, on the very eve of a dominion-provincial conference, when an attempt is being made to bring the 11 governments together on fiscal matters affecting the future of our country, and that the minister should attack, 48 hours before that meeting, a former minister of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources, the present premier of Quebec. I do not think that attempt will help in any way the progress of dominion-provincial relations.
When I was interrupted I was about to say that airstrips were built by the former government at Dawson, Whitehorse, Hay River, Yellowknife and Fort Smith, all along the northwest route. The Canol project was also built during the time of the previous administration. One would think that in the north country absolutely nothing was done prior to 1957. What about the Kitimat-Ter-race railway? What about the extension to the P.G.E. railway, for which the same subsidy to which the minister referred, namely $25,000 per mile, was paid by the previous administration? I could go on and speak of roads running from Edmonton in the direction of Dawson Creek. I have to rely on my memory now as I have no documents before me, but if I had them I am sure I could convince the house that a great deal more had been done in the field to which my hon. friend referred earlier.
There is one other matter for which the present administration seems to be taking credit, the processing of material in this

country. The processing of material in this country started long before the minister was in office and long before his government took office. When the Prime Minister was campaigning in 1957 he took from Hansard and out of context a statement I had made concerning the St. Lawrence seaway to the effect that the St. Lawrence seaway was being built to take iron ore to the United States. No mention was made, however, of the fact that the St. Lawrence seaway was going to create secondary industry and was going to bring primary industry along the shores of the St. Lawrence. If that statement had not been taken out of context it would have been clear that those of us who sat on the other side of the house prior to this administration coming into office were as keenly interested as they are and as every true Canadian is in the processing of Canadian materials in this country.
I am sure that is the objective of all of us who sit in the house, and when it is necessary to export to the United States very often it is because there is not a sufficient market in our own country. The proof of the effect of the development of the St. Lawrence seaway on a number of areas lies in the fact that today natural resources are being processed in various parts of our country.
The Leader of the Opposition dealt at some length with statements made on Saturday by the Prime Minister and also by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources. I shall not add to that other than to refer to the billion dollar program of public works which was put forward in one election campaign and which unquestionably contained the essence of tremendous development by way of employment in the north. As the house knows, little or nothing has been heard about it since.
Finally, I should like to refer to the development in this country both during the war period and the post-war period under the aegis of the Right Hon. C. D. Howe. I do not think history will indicate that at any time has there been a greater development of industry and natural resources than at the time the Right Hon. C. D. Howe was first minister of munitions and supply and later minister of reconstruction and development. There are many people in the country today who would like to see him back in office again and directing the economy of our country.
