speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I have a little difficulty in translating from the French into English. I said to the hon. member at the time that I was not skilled in dialectics. I am not now any more skilled in dialectics. In any event we have heard from the opposition as to what they have done; that Mr. Howe is the greatest man who ever sat in the House of Commons; that they built airfields at Fort Smith and Edmonton. Yes, they did, and I am not going to enter into a debate on that at all. I am trying to make the point objectively that this government did try to meet a situation which was concerning the people of Canada in relation to the ownership of resources. We have taken certain steps and will take other steps to try to push this program forward in order that over the years we can


buy back the ownership in our resources, and maintain them especially in our oil and gas resources of the north.
There were many figures quoted to indicate the extent of investment of nonresidents in our country in the last two years. This is the same point that I have been trying to make, that this great investment in our resources is alarming Canadians. This government is trying to do something about it. I do hope all Canadians will rally behind us in our efforts. I do not believe there are many who would support the hon. member for Port Arthur when he says that we want more investment from the United States. I do not believe he speaks for his party, either. I think the figures are fairly well known. I did not understand the Leader of the Opposition to ask what the percentages were in the northern areas, but I can repeat those figures. In the Arctic islands, 78 per cent are Canadian held and 22 per cent are non-Canadian. This illustrates the fact that we are reversing the percentage that existed in Alberta.
I have made the statement in the house that I did not blame anyone in particular for what happened in Alberta. I am simply saying we do not want it to continue. We welcome foreign investment. However, we want these investors to set up subsidiary companies in which Canadians have an opportunity to participate, and we know there will always be the opportunity for us, as we grow in wealth and accumulated capital, to own these resources. I believe that point has been well covered.
Another point was raised concerning who made the proposal over in the Geneva conference in 1958. Was it something dredged up by the delegates or was it a Canadian proposal, as I said? The best answer to that is the report of the fourth committee on the continental shelf dated April 16, 1958. This is how the secretary of that particular committee describes the events of that day. The delegate from Colombia had spoken, and then we find this:
Mr. Carty (Canada) formally proposed that the committee should recommend to the conference that the results of Its work be embodied in a separate convention relating only to the continental shelf. The purpose of the proposal was to direct attention to the general committee's recommendations contained in paragraph 5 of its report. The fourth committee had made good progress; it should accept its responsibility and formulate, in the form of a convention, the articles which it had adopted. He agreed that the topics discussed at the conference were interrelated and that it would be desirable to decide on the form of instrument for articles 67-73 in the light of the results achieved by other committees.
Then, going on after discussion by the other delegates from the United Kingdom, Yugoslavia, Switzerland, Mexico, Argentina, Chile,

Venezuela, Ceylon, Brazil, the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, India, Israel, the Union of South Africa-just listen to this, Mr. Chairman:
The chairman put to the vote the Canadian proposal, as amended orally by the U.S.S.R. representative.
The Canadian proposal, as amended, was adopted by 39 votes to 6, with 7 abstentions.
The Canadian proposal was put forward on April 16, 1958, and it so happens I was over there as minister of the federal government responsible for the team at the law of the sea convention. I do believe I have the right to say that it was no accident that proposal was put forward. We met every morning to discuss the strategy of that conference. I recall speaking very forcibly on the point that the main consideration we had was to get this one part of the work of the conference clearly into an international convention so it would be of some use to us in case there was a breakdown on any other point. I do not believe my claim was made in any sense as boasting.
There were several other points raised which I think will be straightened out in the record. The first one deals with the statement that I said it was government policy to do certain things on the continental shelf. At the time I objected to that statement, but to make the record absolutely clear I would cite page 6873 of Hansard for July 23, 1960, where the hon. member for Villeneuve said:
So I would suggest the government give serious consideration to granting the provinces the rights to those natural resources on the continental shelf adjoining their own boundaries.
I was not the one who said that, it was the hon. member for Villeneuve. He made the suggestion that we give serious consideration to that matter and naturally, in answer, I said:
This is a matter of government policy and will be declared in due course.
I did not make the statement that these resources should be given back to the provinces because I have no right to make that statement. What I have said in the past is that we have made it very clear that the legal officers of the crown say the continental shelf belongs under federal jurisdiction. If there are any disclaimers to that, there is a proper course to take and that course is up to the persons who feel offended.
I believe those are the main points I have to answer, Mr. Chairman. I am very grateful to the committee for debating this subject of the Liberal versus the Conservative vision so vigorously because I think it will help many Canadians, not only in this committee but outside, to understand what the differences are between us.
Supply-Northern Affairs

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: During the course of the discussion earlier, an hon. member-I believe it was the hon. member for Port Arthur- asked a question about the Yukon. The minister seemed to indicate that he disclaimed jurisdiction. If we have any questions concerning the Yukon, to whom do we direct them?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Yes, I think that is quite correct. The set-up in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon is that we have given jurisdiction to elected councils to look after matters concerning the territories, with the exception of natural resources, education and social welfare for the Indians and Eskimos. The commissioner acts in a dual capacity. When it is a matter that comes under territorial jurisdiction he deals with it without any directions from Ottawa. When it is a matter over which the federal government has jurisdiction he, of course, consults us and is responsible to us for his actions.
This is a very delicate matter in connection with the development of the territory leading finally to the concept of provincial status. In so far as the responsibility of the minister here is concerned, I would suggest it is 100 per cent in connection with matters of federal jurisdiction but in so far as territorial matters are concerned all I can do is relay to the house what is going on there as I see it. I would not want to interfere in their right to decide on such matters as the game laws or the liquor laws which come under their jurisdiction. I can only facilitate any of their actions because everything they do does come under the governor general in council who has to approve all their ordinances. I am not an authority on just what I should be responsible for in the house. I would be glad to discuss any of these matters, as I did with the hon. member for Port Arthur because the case he was discussing was that of an individual criticizing the territorial government. I do not think that I should be required to defend a territorial government or to defend a member. It is a matter between the two and I did not want to get into that discussion.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I have been waiting for some time, for this particular item to be reached, Mr. Chairman. Early in March this year we passed a bill which took over for the Canadian government from United States control a pipe line in the Yukon and the Northwest Territories. At that time there was a great deal of controversy as to what the government intended to do with this pipe line. It was my hope and desire that the Canadian government would take it over as a crown corporation and would operate the pipe line

Supply-Northern Affairs and would also rebuild those roads and airports that were going to serve in the development and the opening up of the particular area.
At that time we were told that because negotiations were being conducted at the time we could not be told what was going to happen to the Canol project. Since then on several occasions I have asked the other minister of northern affairs, the hon. member for Yukon, what the situation was in relation to this matter and he said that he did not know. Now that we have had an opportunity of buying it and have in fact bought it, I should like to know what we are going to do with it and what the disposition of it is. It is now no longer a buying proposition; it is something that the Canadian people own. I think that now is the time to tell us whether we are going to get it as a crown corporation or whether we are going to sell it or lease it to companies as was suggested at the time of the discussion.
I think this has been an opportunity for development in that area. Connected with the projected has been extensive road development, extensive airfield development as well as the pipe line itself. We were told we were getting a real bargain, that we were getting about a $1,700 million proposition for about $600,000, that this was a bargain. I think this type of bargain could and should be used for the development of that area. I am still of the opinion that the best way in which that can be done is through public ownership and operation as a crown corporation.
I was also interested in the statement the minister made about developing the lead and zinc mines in other areas. While I am not familiar with what the background is or what the situation is, I think the minister should bear in mind something that Larry Sefton, district director of district No. 5 of the united steelworkers said a few months ago when they were discussing the Elliot Lake proposition and the uranium industry in general. He made the statement-and I think it is a correct one-that if we do not plan what we were going to do with our natural resources, it is much better to leave those natural resources alone and not touch them at all. There would have been less of a problem at Elliot Lake to the miners, to the people of the community, to the government of Ontario and to the municipal governments that put money into this project, if we had never operated the uranium industry at all. People are going to lose their life savings in the houses they purchased there when no jobs are possible for many of them in the future.


I think we should be giving serious consideration to developing new industries. It is quite true, as the minister said, that if we are going to fit this into our economy, this is the time in which to do it. We must ascertain for ourselves what is the marketing potentiality, what the needs are and then develop a fairly long range program. However, I am not in agreement in any way, shape or form in developing natural resources that are going to be at the expense of the people themselves if we have not a long range program under which we can foresee the sale at reasonable prices of the minerals we are going to produce. Otherwise, it would be much better that we did not operate these mines at all or that we did not do any of the development that is necessary.
I am also interested in another field. I am pleased that the minister has divided his department into two sections. I suggest there should be another section. I come from a part of Ontario that is still in a period of growth, a period in which it is dependent entirely for its existence on its primary natural resources. These resources of minerals such as gold, silver and the other metals and the lumbering industry have been the basis for the development of northern Ontario. This development has all taken place within the last 60 or 70 years.
We have now reached the stage where the development of the natural resources of the nothem area has come to an end. Within the last few weeks in Kirkland Lake we have notice being given of the closing down of two large mines that have been in operation for many years, one of them for 25 years. We have taken the precaution of keeping these properties in production through emergency gold mining assistance and in other ways have assisted them to stay in production. But we have done nothing whatsoever as a government to further the secondary development that is absolutely necessary in order to carry on the second stage. To me it seems rather silly that we should be interested in going into new areas and developing new mines and in going into new areas and developing towns like Frobisher Bay when we have towns much closer that are already there and that are completely dependent on the government for starting the second stage of their development and bringing them into the general economy of the country through the expansion of secondary industry.
This must be the responsibility of the government. If we are going into the production of minerals, into the lumbering industry or any of the other natural resources, I think this must be a planned forage into those industries. I think we must know how far we are going to go, how extensively we are

going to support it, what protection we can give for the lifetime of that particular industry but, particularly in those industries that are not renewable, we should be prepared to start a secondary development so that we shall not have ghost towns all throughout northern Ontario, the north of Quebec and, I imagine, all through northern Canada including the Northwest Territories.
It is all very nice to say that this vision keeps moving farther and farther away. We were greatly impressed in Ontario to find that the people in Toronto bought this because all they ever knew about northern development was that if you bought stock on Bay street you could make a fairly good profit on those stocks and that it was a nice thing to get more mines in production because there was a great deal more money to be made on Bay street in the development of those mines. But they never came north to see what was developed and they were not particularly interested in doing so. They were more interested in getting premiums or in clipping coupons of those that were successful and they wanted to forget about those that were not successful.
If we are going to be honest about the vision in northern Canada-and I think we should be, it seems to me that we are going to be going north, we are going to develop the north; there is no question about that- I think we should consolidate some of the northern development that we have already done. In my opinion, there is no better place in which to live than in northern Ontario where the mines are now starting to close down. Sylvanite will be laying off 300 or 400 men in the next few weeks. Kirkland Lake Minerals will be laying off at the end of this month or on the 31st of this month half of their staff. The other half of the staff will be doing a clean-up operation and then the mine will be completely closed in a very short time.
It seems to me that one of the branches of the department of northern affairs should be a branch that will handle secondary industry. I suggest that the minister give serious consideration to this matter. It is not good enough to leave them trailing all over the country, with public works giving a handout here and northern affairs putting their foot in it in another place and the minister of mines making promises in his jurisdiction and none of them actually facing the problem that must be faced, namely that of secondary industry.
In speaking of natural resources and of northern development, may I say that I think the time has come when we must be realistic about putting secondary industries
Supply-Northern Affairs into northern Ontario. This can be done only on a planned basis by a department that is situated so that it can take advantage of the natural development that flows from primary resources and puts some of that money and some of those resources and some of the development that is possible into secondary industries so that when the one dies, the other is being born and communities are able to continue. It will not impress the people of the Kirkland Lake area and the other mining communities at all to hear about the future development of places like Frobisher and other mining communities when they themselves have no jobs or places to go to or no secondary industry in sight.
I think the minister should give serious consideration to this matter of secondary development which is a natural offshoot of primary development of our natural resources. While it may be difficult to convince a Conservative government that this should be done, because it means economical planning and the taking of some money out of the pockets of those who have been scavengers throughout the ages on both the lumber and mining industries, some money must flow back into the development of secondary industries. If we offer the considerations which have been offered in other countries to develop secondary industries we can have secondary industries in our northern areas of Ontario and Quebec.
It is not good enough to say that we will do it five years from now. As far as Kirkland Lake is concerned two of the producing mines are now closing in the next few weeks and I am sure others will follow because some of them have been in production for 25 to 30 years and this is the lifetime, in the main, of these industries. The protection we gave to the forest industry has not made it possible for us to have a continuing industry in that field either, so that secondary industries are the only answer we have to this matter of solving the problem which arises after you complete the first stages of development in the field of natural resources.
There is another problem which affects us, and that is the matter of a seaport on James bay which is not the responsibility of any department of government. We have raised this on almost all the estimates but we are always told it belongs to somebody else. Surely, Mr. Chairman, this belongs at least partly to the department of northern affairs because this is one of the methods, in my opinion, by which we will be able to bring in secondary industries to areas which to a

Supply-Northern Affairs great extent are now devoid of natural resources, and at the same time it will start a flow into that area of natural resources from other areas.
I think the minister is fully aware of the potentialities we have in the Hudson bay and James bay areas which will flow into the heart of industrial Canada and the Toronto area if we are able to develop a port which will make it feasible and economical to produce the iron ore and other minerals in the area to the point where they can be transported to the companies and the areas which will use them. If we do that I think also in the process we will be building secondary industry all along the route which will follow from the fact that we will be supplying finished products, the things which are necessary to develop new areas, mining equipment, all the feeder equipment which will go into production. We will be able to produce that all along the line and this will in turn be a partial solution to the problem which is now faced by those areas which only a few years ago were part of our northern development and which are now nearly devoid of any secondary industry unless it can get it from the reflection of the vision this government has.

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am not an historian but I want to speak on this item. I always feel at home in tall timber. We discussed this thoroughly on the bill to set up the new Department of Forestry so I will be brief. I think it is safe to say that this is
Supply-Northern Affairs the last time the estimates of this branch will come before us as a branch of this department because next year I presume the item will be a main one in the estimates of the department of forestry.
We hope that as a result of the conference on resources for tomorrow there will be an agreement on certain principles between the government and certain provinces respecting policies concerning the development of forest research and forestry in general. We appreciate the work done by this department and particularly the forest products laboratory which produced many splendid booklets which I have in my hand. When the department is well under way we hope the branch will have ample funds to extend its work in connection with keeping in contact with the lumber industry and especially small operators. Despite the good work done in the past small operators did not know the information was available but knowledge of it is more widespread today.
I shall deal with an immediate problem that can be tackled in the immediate future through efforts on the part of the federal and provincial governments to prevent losses from fires that are occurring even at the present time. The Nelson News of July 21 mentioned that in the Kootenays at the present time approximately 2,000 men are fighting fires and a more recent report indicates that 10,000 acres of timber are on fire. The expenditure on the part of the provincial government is very heavy. There is a worse state of affairs in the region north of Kamloops and to some extent in central British Columbia. I see by the press that there are heavy fire losses in other parts of Canada.
I am keen on this question because I witnessed some bad fires. My first experience was that of being the youngest man on a fire fighting crew in the early days of this century when I was given the job of leading 10 young ladies through the mountains in the dark and depositing them safely at a lakeside some 10 miles away and I have seen many fires since. I stood on a mountain and saw timber in a valley 15 miles long and three miles wide completely destroyed in three hours; 200 million feet of commercial or near commercial timber almost completely destroyed, nothing left but charred stumps and trees killed by the heat. These experiences have led to my keen interest.
Fire prevention is not just a matter of more funds but a question of co-operation between the federal and provincial governments, various government departments and other agencies in the province and even in the

Supply-Northern Affairs municipalities in some cases, and the organization and better mobilization of presently available resources.
I do hope that one of the first things this conference on resources for tomorrow tackles is an immediate problem, something that can be done, as it were, overnight, compared with forestry laboratory research, forestry research or forestry fire protection reseach; that is, some program and planning which, as I said before, will enable us to organize the capacity we have today to fight forest fires in Canada and to mobilize our resources. I suggest that we should have an over-all national policy in this respect that provides for the throwing into a forest fire situation first of all the local resources in manpower, materials and equipment, and when it is obvious that that is not sufficient, then the provincial resources come into play and then finally if necesary we can throw in the national resources.
In the national resources I include the armed forces. I think it is absolutely ridiculous that we should have thousands of men in training at the present time, particularly those men in engineering corps and certain infantry units in the army who could be spared for a month or two, if necessary, to fight fires, and not use them. We have a situation in British Columbia where the armed forces of the federal gov-vernment could be used. The Department of National Defence should be willing to co-operate with the provincial, regional and local authorities to use the armed forces, whether it is the air force transporting troops, or troops from the infantry or other services, and throw them into a certain area when required to build roads and to assist the local people in fighting the fires which are raging at the present time. The experience would be a good thing for our armed forces. It would be good practice for them in meeting emergency situations and dealing with problems. Very often the problem has to be met under very difficult circumstances of rough terrain with difficulties in respect of transportation of food, men and equipment, and so on.
As I said before, I am going to be quite brief, but I do suggest that one of the first questions that should be considered by the resources for tomorrow conference should be the organization and mobilization of all our resources in Canada as the result of co-operation among the federal and provincial governments and the regional and local authorities in an effort to limit as much as we can the destruction of our forests by fire which is so devastating from year to year and particularly at this time
[Mr. Herridge.l
while we are discussing the estimates of the forestry branch of this department.

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: I have a question or two for the minister in connection with this division of his department. I take it that this is the division which is going to be transferred to the new department of forestry.

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
First of all, I should like to thank the hon. member for Kootenay West for his kind words to the members of the forestry branch and both -research and forest products laboratory, because I do not think there is a group of people more deserving of the thanks of their fellow Canadians. I should like to add my words of appreciation in the committee at this time of the officials of this branch who will soon be moving to the new department.
The hon. member for Kootenay West raised the question of forest fires. When I introduced second reading of the forestry bill I suggested that something could be done in setting up reservoirs of trained personnel and equipment. I should like to inform the hon. member and the committee that just last week end there was a meeting in Oris-kany, Quebec, of representatives of the forest industry, the province of Quebec, the province of Ontario, and the province of New Brunswick, represented by ministers; also representatives of the armed services, the army and air force, wondering and working out plans that I hope will be put before the new minister in connection with the proposal that I originally hinted at when I was speaking on second reading of the forestry bill and which has been amplified to a degree by the hon. member for Kootenay West.
I think I can say on my part that until this branch is removed from my jurisdiction I will push as hard as I can to see that everything is done in the form of planning for the new minister; that he will have research work that we have done, at least planning for research work that we have done, and planning

better forest fire co-operation with the provinces. All these plans will be turned over to the minister and I will not stop because the branch is leaving me sometime this year.
The hon. member for Laurier asked for details of what is being done with this particular branch. The actual divisions that will go over to the new department from the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources are: forest research division; forest products research division; forest operations division and the administrative division. From agriculture there will go just one division composed of the two sections, forest entomology and forest pathology. In addition to this, there will have to be built up an administrative corps under which these various branches will operate. I do believe there has to be an economics section and a section on marketing to co-operate with the Department of Trade and Commerce, and some administrative officials.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I want to support very strongly the point made by the hon. member for Kootenay West about the armed forces. It seems to me it could be very much a part of their training to have them work in fire prevention, especially since it would require their movement at speed to different parts of the country. If the minister runs into any difficulty in getting co-operation in working out such a plan and such a task force, I would suggest to him that he compare, at least in the cabinet and with the Minister of National Defence, the efficacy of the changing of the guard out on parliament hill with the contribution that a force of equal size and of equal training, but in a much more utilitarian field, could play in fire fighting assistance.
The hon. member for Kootenay West has fires in his area similar to those which we have had in northwestern Ontario recently. The problem of the Ontario provincial fire service is not one of bad organization but has to do with the fact that they cannot keep up to strength to master completely all fire problems on any kind of a permanent
Supply-Northern Affairs basis. Last year was a wonderful year in Ontario from a fire point of view in that because of a combination of weather and other factors there was very little in the way of threat. This year the situation is much different, and I have great sympathy with the provincial authorities and the problems they face.
In the Canadian army we have a corps of men whom we can only look upon as being primarily to defend our own country and who could form a kind of task force which could come into the picture when a fire problem arose and because of the experience they would have they would gain very much in a military way. If we contemplate fighting the Russians some day, I imagine most of the fighting will take place in the boreal forest area, and the experience gained in the bush, with all its tribulations, fighting fires is something that I think our army could well afford.
I have noticed in the press the magnificent manoeuvres that are taking place near Petawawa at the present time and the cost to the taxpayers. I am pleased to think our soldiers are being trained but I also think of how comparable in worth the training would be that they would get in moving to danger areas where there are fires. That is why I should like to support very strongly the suggestion that the minister take the lead through this branch in seeing such a force developed.
I should like to ask the minister several questions about the branch. What is going to be done about the library services and facilities for the new forestry department? I am not critical of the forestry branch library. The last time I was there a few years ago it struck me as being a fair though not an excellent library to serve the specific branch, but if we are going to have a forestry department it seems to me it has to be much larger.
The minister is probably aware that from a research point of view the papers and documentation on file now in the Department of Agriculture are much more complex and go much deeper in terms of classification than much of the general forestry literature whether it has to do with economics of forest management or silviculture. Therefore I should like to know what the plans are for the library service in the new department and just what role is now going to be played by the library that now exists in the forestry branch. If, as the minister indicates, the new department is going to be the leading research organization in Canada for forestry in all its aspects I suggest we need more space than we have at present, more librarians and real
7062	HOUSE OF
Supply-Northern Affairs planning in this field. I should like to know what the minister can tell us about this matter.
There is one other piece of information I should like to have. How much time was given by the foresters of the forestry branch to assistance of the Indian affairs branch in relation to Indian lands in the last year or so? Is there under consideration at the present time any arrangement with the Indian affairs branch that would lead to greater provision of the services of professional foresters to the Indian affairs branch than exists now?

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Before I say a word on this item, may I be permitted to welcome the new premier of New Brunswick, whose presence has been noted in the gallery.
This item has to do with the contribution to the province of New Brunswick for assistance in a program designed to combat spruce budworm infestation in accordance with an agreement entered into by Canada and the province. The minister will recall that a few years ago there were some unfortunate instances connected with the spraying operation. Certain streams and certain ponds were infected and the fish were being killed. Could the minister advise this committee if the necessary precautionary measures have been taken to avoid a repetition of such unfortunate incidents?
It seems to me that I recall reading an article in one of the New Brunswick newspapers a few days ago in which it was stated that certain streams had been depleted of sport fish. I believe trout was mentioned in that instance. The main reason for this was the spraying operation. I am not against the spraying of New Brunswick's forests to protect them from budworm infestation, but I do believe certain precautionary measures should be taken. I wonder if the minister could advise the committee if this matter has been looked into?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Yes, this has been a matter of considerable interest to both governments. In the past the spraying has been done on the basis of using 1| pounds of d.d.t. per acre. We have been in consultation with the Department of Fisheries here, and of course the same department in New Brunswick, and this year in areas close to streams we have decided to use only one-quarter pound of d.d.t. per acre. The fisheries people advise this will not do too much harm to fish, and of course I accept their advice. I think there is a reasonable chance that this compromise will succeed in slowing down
Supply-Northern Affairs the budworms and at the same time not do too much damage to the fish.

Item agreed to.
National museum of Canada-
302.	Administration, operation and maintenance, $736,904.

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: I hope the minister can give us a statement on how the national museum has been adjusting to the problems it had in the last two or three years, the scandal, if I might call it that, within the management. I should like to know, especially, about the performance of some of these central figures in the Rousseau charges, and generally how the museum is coming along now, especially since it now has the building all to itself and is in a position to get moving along in a more constructive pattern. I should like to know whether the government is still searching for a senior appointment amongst the French-Canadians of the population. I should like to know what balance is being sought in connection with that particular matter in order to give French-Canadians some representation at the senior level that they had on such a temporary basis before what was, in effect, the dismissal of Dr. Rousseau.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
First of all, I think the committee will agree with me that there was hardly a scandal down at the museum. It is true that one or two newspapers had headlines which made it look as if there were something very odd going on down there. Fortunately, in the interests of justice and fair play, they stopped that and I am very grateful to them for doing so.
At the present time the director of the museum and the permanent head of the natural history museum is Dr. Russell. He is also the acting head of the human history side of the museum. Recently we have been able to recruit a topnotch person by the name of Mr. Wilson, who will be the assistant director of the human history and natural history side. We are looking forward to gradually straightening out the administrative problems that have arisen in the museum.
I should like at this time to make certain that everyone knows some of our thinking on the museum. The national museum is the place where we keep a record of those things dealing with our natural history and human history. This museum has worked under a
[Mr. Chevrier.l

very severe handicap because it had to share the building with the geological survey of Canada and the national art gallery.
After many long years the building has now come back to the museum. Certain repair work must be done to modernize the museum for better use. I want to make this point clear. The primary purpose of the museum is to collect our history. However, an important secondary purpose is to make this history accessible and available to all Canadians. It is extremely difficult to move every Canadian to Ottawa. Therefore the museum has done wonderful work in the scientific field in preparing booklets and brochures on various parts of the work we are doing. Indeed, I should like them to push this work further.
Through the medium of television, for example, I should like to be able to take and make alive the exhibits we have there in a dynamic form and send them all across the country through the means of television. In the replanning of the Victoria building I hope that space will be set up for a television studio. I also hope that the various television companies, in trying to achieve their 55 per cent Canadian content, will realize that the best entertainment over a period of years is education and that the great knowledge collected by great scientists in this building will become the real heritage of people all across the country by having it taken to them in the form of television. There are other ways of taking museums to the people. I do not want to bore the committee with details but I will say this. I am quite proud of the way in which the museum is taking hold of this task and with the great ability and the great sense of scientific accuracy possessed by the staff, I am sure the Canadian people, when they have the museum taken to them, will be seeing some of the best examples of the collection of knowledge that we have any place in the world.

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
In view of the fact that historically Conservative parties have always looked upon nations as national museums and the parties in question as the curators of those museums, the government should meet its greatest success in the administration of this national museum of ours. I think there have been some improvements since the Conservatives came to power. That is one of the branches of the various departments for the improvement of whose administration I give them great credit, although it has been slow. However, I presume it is in line with their historical role in history.
However, I rose particularly to deal with a matter that is of particular concern to people in other museums across Canada and those people who are interested in preserving

the archaeological finds and artifacts and other things of the past. In this connection I wish to quote briefly from the report of the committee on mines, forests and waters of the last session in connection with the museum. This report starting at page 671 of Votes and Proceedings of July 6, 1959 reads as follows:
Your committee recommends that the government examine the adequacy of present legislation and regulations concerning protection of archaeological discoveries and artifacts, and their export from Canada. Such examination should include liaison with the provinces for exchange of information on archaeological discoveries and for uniformity of protective legislation throughout Canada.
I should be interested in knowing what has been done to give effect to that recommendation on the part of the committee because of the interest that is shown in this question by persons across Canada. My attention was drawn quite recently to an article in Maclean's magazine of July 4, 1959. It is written by Fred Bodsworth and it is entitled "The scandal of our lost art treasures". In it he goes to great lengths to indicate how our lost art treasures are going to the United States particularly and in some cases to other nations because apparently we have not in the national museums, the provincial museums or among private persons the initiative to make certain that these treasures are not lost to Canada. I want to quote just a few comments made in this article because they -impressed me greatly and in order to emphasize the importance of this question to the committee:
For 200 years such treasures of Canadian art and history have been pouring unnoticed out of our country into the museums and private collections of the United States and Europe. They have included not only historical treasures of our own pioneer era, but also vast quantities of primitive Indian and Eskimo art-irreplaceable examples of the now forgotten crafts of our first Canadians.
Then he goes on to deal with the places to which these things have gone. He states:
The Detroit institute of art has a collection of French Canadiana (church sculpture, silver and pioneer furniture) much choicer and comprehensive than anything in Canada, including French Canada.
New York's museum of the American Indian alone has seventy superb examples of a much-sought type of abstract, wooden, Eskimo mask; in all Canada there are fewer than a dozen comparable specimens.
Then he goes on to say this:
But the world's biggest Haida argillite collection is a privately owned one in Florida, its 527 specimens probably outranking all Canadian collections combined.
The art's earliest and most primitive period, prior to the 1830's, is represented in Canada by only one specimen-a pipe in the Hudson's Bay Company museum in Winnipeg. But there are scores of specimens dating back to that period-in the
Supply-Northern Affairs Paris museum of man, the Peabody museum of Massachusetts and the U.S. national museum in Washington.
While we neglect taking care of these treasures, he goes on further to say this: Meanwhile collectors from other countries, especially the United States, were overrunning Canada and carting our heritage away by the boxcar load.
I know that the protection of Canadian archaeological discoveries and artifacts is not the sole responsibility or jurisdiction of the national museum. However, I urge that everything possible be done by this government to interest provincial museums and historical associations. I think it is an excellent thing to get the co-operation of local historical associations in connection with the preservation of these interesting relics with respect to our history and former civilization on this continent. I know that our own historical society-I refer to the West Kootenay historical society; and I have never been backward in saying that we are extremely progressive in West Kootenay in many respects-has been greatly interested in making certain of the preservation of Indian relics and things of that sort, of early relics of the pioneer settlements in the fur trading days and the early lumbering days, of the early agricultural settlements, and so on.
I am sorry to know that the only specimen of a Kootenay canoe in existence in Canada was brought from the Kootenays to the national museum, was hung from the ceiling and was allowed to perish from lack of care. One morning when the caretaker went into the museum he found it had fallen to the floor and had broken into many fragments. It is a most unfortunate thing that this canoe, which represents a type of canoe that is found only in two places of the world, namely on the interior lakes in the Kootenays and on a small lake in northern Siberia, was allowed to perish in the national museum because of lack of care.
I mention that matter because this occurrence was greatly regretted by people who were interested in this matter in my district. I am glad to know that I obtained a good photograph of it before it was allowed to collapse and fall to the floor. The situation arose because of lack of a certain moisture content in the air in the building and because of lack of protection of the surface so that the moisture would not evaporate and it would not become so brittle that it would disintegrate.
Before I sit down I also want to bring to the attention of the committee the comments that were made by my leader, namely the hon. member for Assiniboia who I hope will

Supply-Northern Affairs be national leader of the C.C.F. in Canada. On page 1105 of the committee report appears the following:

This deals with the promise I made that I would make a study of what was going on in the various provinces. In the national parks we have complete power to prohibit removal of these artifacts. In Indian reserves, under the Indian Act, we also have power to restrict the removal, acquisition of title and trespass. In the Yukon and Northwest Territories, under the amendment we have brought about in the last two years, we are required to obtain permission for control of the minister of northern affairs for their export.
Here is the report for the provinces. Newfoundland, no regulations. Nova Scotia, no regulations. Prince Edward Island, no regulations. New Brunswick, the historic sites protection act 1954, amended 1958. This regulates the designation of sites, issuance of permits and establishment of an advisory

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is a subject which lends itself to extended statements but I shall confine myself to what I think are salient points. First of all the government recognizes as did the standing committee on mines, forests and waters, that a determined effort has to be made to increase the tourist business in Canada, not only with respect to the question of trade and commerce to reduce the adverse trade balance but also to ensure the recognition of this industry as a basic industry.
The first thing we did was to increase the amount of direct advertising in newspapers and magazines. This increase for the first time raises the amount of advertising slightly beyond what it was before. It is only fair to point out that the inflation in the advertising costs results in not very much over-all space increase.
Second, we have set up the office in Chicago. We had hoped to set one up in San Francisco as well but we had to live within the terms of our budget and make our contribution in that field. Therefore we were not able to get the office in San Francisco going.

I wish to briefly discuss with the committee something in which I know they will be interested. I refer to the relative merits of advertising over the establishment of offices and other techniques. I know that advertising is very effective in bringing in an increasing number of requests for information. I cannot deny that the effects of the advertising is being carefully evaluated year by year. Every step the advertising agencies can make to prove the effect of our advertising is being taken. However, we have no clear-cut way of evaluating the relative merits of advertising over other forms of inducing tourists to come to this country.
I hold in my hand a page out of a recent Sunday edition of the Chicago Tribune. Hon. members will be able to see that it contains three large beautifully coloured pictures taken along the Alaska highway and a map showing how the people of the United States can get to Alaska. How did this article happen to get into the Chicago Tribune's weekly supplement? The answer is that one of our staff working in the Chicago office became acquainted with members of the staff of the Tribune and I suppose through his enthusiasm and providing them with pictures was able to sell them the idea that their readers would be interested in knowing about the highway that runs into Alaska, the type of scenery that is found along the highway and how to get there. This illustrates one way in which the tourist offices can achieve results.
Third, I wish to mention that for a number of years we have carried out a special program of advertising in an effort to induce people on the eastern seaboard of the United States to go into the four Atlantic provinces. This inducement has been successful to a remarkable degree particularly in the provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia which are not separated by water from the road system of the United States. This program has resulted in a sizeable increase each year in the tourist revenue of those provinces.
This brings to mind something I discussed with the standing committee and that is the need for a similar type of program of advertising with respect to the whole of Canada, centering the program around the fact that in every province the trans-Canada highway is completed or soon to be completed. Personally I should like to see a special campaign inaugurated that would point out to all Canadians the completed parts of the trans-Canada highway and the beautiful attractions that are found tributary to the highway.
Each province has a number of attractions that it would like to make known to all Canadians and tourists coming to this country from the United States. I therefore hope there

will be some agreement reached between the provinces and the federal government with respect to a special program of advertising emphasizing the trans-Canada highway linking Canada from east to west and associated with this campaign I hope, too, that the attractions in the northern parts of our provinces will be made known to the travellers along that highway.
I wish to put in a special plug, if I may, for the people at the end of the road to Yellowknife which will be opened this fall and on behalf of the people of Whitehorse where so much is being done to build up the tourist industry. It is not without interest that reports which have been made public recently about development of the north show that the report dealing with Alaska puts at the head of the list that the leading industry of Alaska in the near future will be the tourist industry. The Sandford report dealing with Saskatchewan also puts the tourist industry at a very high level.
I would suggest to the committee that the importance of this industry is being very widely accepted, and we have to draft plans that will help push this thing forward with the utmost efficiency. Therefore, I would like to complete that work by saying that I should like to see a program that makes Canadians aware of the trans-Canada facilities that are available nearby and particularly the attractions of the Northwest Territories and the Yukon, leading on to Alaska. If we do this I think there is a tremendous number of adventurous Americans who, when they realize there are good roads, good accommodation and tremendous scenic attractions at the end, will want to see their 49th state.
The final thing is this question of European tourist trade. In Europe today there is a relaxation of restrictions, particularly in the United Kingdom, which makes it possible for Canada to move into this market and see whether we cannot induce people to use the cheaper fares that now exist to come to Canada, just as Canadians are using those cheaper air fares to go to those countries of Europe this year. The director of the travel bureau is going to Europe to visit the high commissioner in London and various European countries to talk to their tourist officials to see whether there could not be a program worked out whereby we would in some measure begin to reverse the trend which has become apparent in the last few years of Canadians going to Europe. We do not want to stop that but we do want to try to get more Europeans to come to see Canada, and to make known what is available to them. I do not know whether this summary answers what the hon. member for Laurier has in mind.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I feel this is such an important subject that the views of hon. members should be heard. From his opening statement in introducing his estimates and from his statement in the committee of mines, forests and waters last year and from his statements outside the house, it is evident that the minister has a very keen appreciation of the value of the tourist industry and of the development of the industry in Canada. But this, I feel, is a commercial problem and the technique of dealing with it must be borrowed from the field of commerce and the practices of the market place must be common to all our thinking in endeavouring to develop effective means of drawing more business into Canada for the tourist industry.
I appreciate very much the fact that the minister is aware of the value and of the necessity of increasing the number of offices we have in the United States, in addition to an increase in the amount of advertising we do in that area, because advertising of itself is not enough. Even if we were to double our present budget, which I think we ought to do as quickly as possible, anyone in the field of commerce realizes that advertising alone is not enough to sell products; a sales force is essential to follow through on the effects achieved by the advertising program. Advertising softens up, but the sale is undertaken by personal contact. Therefore, a sales force and a travel office can be seen as a branch office of Canadian tourism in the United States, and the staff of those offices should be seen as a sales force for Canadian tourism. Unless the techniques of commercial salesmanship are used those offices are of no value whatever, or at least not the value that they might be.
The minister mentioned the photographs in the Chicago Tribune recently. I would hope that it is common practice of the staff of our travel offices in the United States to constantly endeavour to secure this kind of publicity. If they are not trying to do that they might as well be brought home and be replaced by people who are aware of the necessity of this type of salesmanship and will make it one of the first essentials ol their approach to increasing our tourist trade.
I feel that the offices must be considered as sales offices. This is their primary and most important function. The people in those offices must be endeavouring to reach out to our customers, the tourists for Canada, the people of the United States, whether it be service clubs, fraternal organizations, associations of professional people, audiences of

Supply-Northern Affairs Americans that may be reached through any media whatever, in co-operation with Canadian travel organizations, Canadian tourist organizations, Canadian organizations having to do with hotel accommodations, motel associations, Canadian restaurant associations. They must endeavour to sell the ideas of a packaged travel program to groups of people, by making arrangements to make travel in Canada attractive by providing easy and inexpensive opportunities for people to come to Canada, with the co-operation of all those groups in this country that are interested in providing for tourists.
What we want is an imaginative program. We want vigorous people, and they should realize one thing above all, that they are salesmen and they have to get out and reach the customer. They cannot sit in offices and wait for customers to come to them. As long as that concept is realized, then those offices that we have plus those that we add will be worth while. But unless that concept is to be used and put in practice throughout the United States-I hope in far more places than just the three offices, the two now established and the third one contemplated in San Francisco-we shall not be as successful in that effort as we should be. The committee on mines, forests and waters last year recommended Cleveland, Boston and other locations. If these offices are established, then we ought to make sure that the people who go into them have a very clear conception of what their responsibility will be and that they are going to the United States to sell Canadian tourism.
Further than that, the committee recommended last year-and I think the minister is very conscious of this requirement also- that the concept of the responsibility of the tourist bureau be enlarged to include the promotion, in co-operation with the provinces, of increased tourist travel by Canadians in Canada, because while the United States expenditure in Canada increased by $10 million over the previous year, the fact is that Canadians are spending half a billion dollars in foreign countries on travel while foreign visitors are spending $353 million, or thereabouts, in this country. That is not satisfactory.
The minister recognizes that and I believe in his recognition he must be supported by the government and by hon. members to see that the expansion that he has envisioned will come into being and come into being quickly. But particularly, I would suggest that in reviewing how we are going to take advantage of the expanded facilities that are provided we realize that this is a commercial problem; it is a selling problem and the only techniques


that are going to be effective in any measure whatever are to see that the people we send into the field are salesmen and when they get there that they sell by every means possible and if they are not capable of doing it they should be brought home and replaced by others in Canada who are.

speechtext:
I think I have been very restrained, indeed, this afternoon and not as loquacious as the hon. member for Laurier on occasion.
The tourist industry is a matter of great importance to Canada and is increasing substantially in importance right across the country as people discover the garden of Eden in Canada.
I see, regardless of cuts in other respects, that the vote this year is $2,687,178, which is an increase over last year. I am very pleased to see this increase because I think it is a good investment in the circumstances.
The department is engaged in the function of answering inquiries, which is a very necessary one, in issuing publications and in advertising in various forms. I think these are all worth-while activities which have borne fruit in past years.
I think something more than that is required to achieve success so far as our tourist industry is concerned, namely co-operation with local organizations, with the people of the country, as it were, tourist bureaux, chambers of commerce, tourist camp operators, persons who cater to the tourist industry in various ways, and particularly those engaged on a somewhat smaller scale in the more remote places. You do not have to advertise to get people to go to Banff, Lake Louise and other internationally known resorts. As a result of my experience I find that an increasing number of people want to do two things. First, they want to go to our national parks and their remote and less developed areas. Second, they want to go to the smaller tourist camp operations in the remote areas away from the centres of civilization.
I should like to suggest three things before I sit down. First, it would be a good idea, and I make this suggestion with the best of intentions, for the travel bureau to keep in touch with the operators of smaller tourist camps throughout the country and get suggestions from them as to advertising and publicity and information as to the comments that are heard from tourists from other parts of Canada or from the United States or other countries as to what they enjoy, what they would prefer or what they miss and so on.

Second, I suggest it would be an excellent thing to keep these people, and I know a lot of them, well informed of the work of the bureau and supplied with information to keep them in touch with the industry in their own province and in the rest of Canada as far as possible.
As to my third suggestion, I find that generally speaking tourist camp operators are all in the same circumstances as the hon. member for Kootenay West, always short of funds. I know people with excellent sites and good fishing and that sort of thing and yet they lack the capital to expand their business to meet the opportunities today. I suggest that the minister bring that particularly to the attention of the Minister of Finance because in the last year or two I have had many complaints from persons operating small tourist camps against local banks because of their tight money policy, shall I say, although I do not really like the term. The banks do not seem to have much confidence in the development of our tourist industry. I know of one particular case in my constituency where the value of the operation to date is over $200,000 and the bank looked down its nose at a request for a loan of $5,000 over a period of a year in order to carry out certain developments.
I suggest that the government should include tourist camp operations within the ambit of the Industrial Development Bank Act or similar legislation. I have had this matter brought to my attention by a number of those in my constituency who are interested in the industry and by others in southeastern British Columbia. With these few remarks I will take my seat, I presume much to the satisfaction of the hon. member for Laurier.

I am not saying this in order to play politics because I am interested particularly in this department which affects so many working

branches of the government in which a fulltime minister could take an interest and render a great service. I express the hope that at an early date the government will see fit to designate a full-time secretary of state who will occupy that office for as long as this government is in power. What I am saying should not be considered to be any reflection on the present incumbent. So far as I am concerned, it does not matter very much if he occupies the post or someone else does. I am quite pleased with the manner in which he has carried out his functions so far.
I do not intend to say anything about the civil service commission this evening. I feel there is a very good reason why we should not say too much about this. The minister has already indicated that at the next session we will have an opportunity of discussing a new civil service act. It is unfortunate, once again, that although this legislation was forecast in the speech from the throne, we did not get this committee started in the early days of the session. I am sure, however, the government will have no reason for not establishing this committee at the earliest possible date next session.
I am particularly interested, Mr. Chairman, in the report of the royal commission on patents, industrial design and copyright. The minister did make a statement a while ago as to the report on patents which was presented last year. There was also the report on copyright which was presented in 1957 and the report on industrial design which was presented in 1958.
To go backwards, I start with patents. I understand that at this time we cannot hope to change the patent law; nor do I expect that this government or any other government at the next session, in accordance with the report of the royal commission, could produce a Patent Act which would be satisfactory even to any hopeful beginner in patent law. I do not expect action. I am reasonable about this matter. But I expect that the government will listen to representations from various groups and interested parties and will give an opportunity to a committee, perhaps at the next session or a subsequent one, namely a joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons.
If my memory serves me rightly, I think it was in 1935 that a joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons made a general study of the Patent Act. That procedure worked out well. In studying the project of a new Patent Act or a new patent law, if such a thing is in the mind of the government, after representations have been made I hope that any new legislation will be

submitted to a joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons, which committee I think should formulate a law as to patents which will last for at least some time.
We have had a great many changes in legislation as to patents and trade marks in the past 25 years. In a small country like Canada it is really an extravagance to have what is going on at the present time. I am a practising lawyer and I have never been able to catch up with the changes. It took me some time to learn something about the 1935 Patent Act. We have had many amendments since then and it is now suggested that we should have a new patent law. We had a Trade Marks Act which was revised only a few years ago. Now there are suggestions to be made about designs.
I think that any steps which should be taken in the future should be constructive ones. I hope the government will take its time so that any law which we adopt will be a more or less permanent institution. This country cannot afford to change its law on trade marks, industrial design, and patents every 25 years.
However, I would point out that in the case of the copyright law this report was submitted two years ago. The Copyright Act is one that has not changed over the years and it requires real revision and real amendment. I would suggest to the government that it immediately institute some study with regard to the copyright law. I urge the minister, through his officials and interested parties, to seek to draft a proposed copyright law so that at the earliest opportunity parliament may consider it. As to the copyright law, there are many facets which are undesirable. In connection with any of these laws may I say this, and it will appeal to the government; it appeals to many of us and it appeals to the government, apparently. In connection with these laws it is time for us to look after interests of Canadians. We always speak about looking after the interest of Canadians. In patent matters, industrial design matters and copyright matters, while we should respect as much as possible international agreements, we should first consider Canadian interests.
One does not need to be a student of statistics to understand the present situation. One can look at the grants of patents, for example, and it will be seen that a small proportion of them are granted to Canadians. I think the figure is 1,506 out of a total of about 24,000, which is a small proportion while the United States proportion is 64 per cent as against 6 per cent Canadian and 10 per cent in the United Kingdom. Therefore in drafting laws of that kind in the future,
Supply-Secretary of State we should be extremely careful to see to it that we protect the interests of Canadians and also that we are not merely passing laws to help people who are foreign to this country, although they are our friends, providing patent protection which may be of some use to them but which is detrimental to us.
By that I am not saying that the Patent Act as it stands now is detrimental to the Canadian people. However, I say that there are some aspects of the law which are not helpful to Canadians. They create a sort of tariff bar against Canadians. Our law does not protect Canadians as it should. When this matter comes up for consideration on another occasion I should be glad to express my views on it. However, I urge the government to go carefully about redrafting the Patent Act and to consult not just one group but all the interested parties who may want to make submissions, even though we have a report from a royal commission. A report from a royal commission may be a fine guide but I still think that the government and the members of this house must take responsibility for passing legislation which will be of the greatest benefit to the people of this country.
In connection with this matter I was going to say that while we have a technical report from the royal commission on patents, copyright and industrial designs, their field did not cover administration. I come back to this matter before this committee because I think it is the government's responsibility to seek some better way in which to administer these three branches of the Department of Secretary of State. At some time I am sure a government will decide that there should be a head over these three departments who will have the rank of deputy minister. At the present time we have branches under the secretary of state such as the Queen's printer who has the rank of deputy minister. We have the chief electoral officer and we have others such as the dominion archivist. But in the case of patents, trade marks and designs, these men do not hold office with the rank of deputy minister. They are under the undersecretary of state. While that situation is all very well, I do not think this important branch should be without its own head reporting directly to the minister.
I urge the government to consider this suggestion because this was not a matter for the royal commission to consider. I think the government will be instituting an important advance in the interest of the department of patents, trade marks and copyright if it would establish such a department under such a head. I think the Prime Minister will agree with me that matters arising under the patent law, the trade mark law and the

Supply-Secretary of State copyright law require a head who will understand and be responsible for these acts. I know that is the feeling of solicitors and counsel who act before the department. They feel there should be one head over this department, with a director for each branch. This is a suggestion I make to the secretary of state and I hope it will be given further consideration in the near future.
I know that the question of a building for the patent office, the trade mark office and the copyright office is not exactly within the purview of the secretary of state. However, this is an opportunity to tell the Prime Minister and the Minister of Public Works at the same time that it is not satisfactory to go to these departments in No. 8 building, that wooden building out at the farm. It would do some of the members of the government good, in connection with some duties relating to patents or trade marks, to go running around the halls in No. 8 building, in order to find out how difficult the problem is. These are departments to which the public has access all the time and in which business is being carried on for the public in various parts of the country. I feel that a building should be provided as soon as possible in the vicinity of the parliament buildings-for example, on Sussex street near the research council-where all the offices of the patents, trade marks and copyright divisions would be concentrated. I will reserve any further remarks to the separate items.

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: I have a few brief remarks I should like to make at this time. I do not think any of us are ready to complain about the person holding the office of Acting Secretary of State, but I do want to say, particularly since the Prime Minister is in the committee, that it would seem to me it is a mistake to keep a minister in an acting position on almost an indefinite basis. I would suggest to the Prime Minister that it might be very much in order for him either to appoint the present person as a permanent minister as ministers go and remove him from the necessity of acting as the Acting Secretary of State-

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: It will not be long before you achieve that.

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I am not going to make any forecasts. Time will decide these things. I notice the Prime Minister smiling, and he was smiling some time ago as soon as I started to say this and I expected he would.


But I do feel that since the Prime Minister is in a position to do something about it it would be a very good thing to have a regular secretary of state instead of a genial and competent Acting Secretary of State on what appears to be a rather permanent basis.
The Ilsley royal commission was asked to inquire into the whole question of patents, copyrights and trade marks and these reports have now been made to the government. I would hope that appropriate action can be taken at an early date. It is a long time since I have said anything in this house on the question of patents, but I do feel that patents in the past have been used as a method of obtaining artificially high prices; that they have been used to maintain a monopoly position in many instances; that they have been used to prevent competition; and that they have been a very heavy burden on the general public.
The purpose of that inquiry, I take it, was to revise the Patent Act and these other acts so as to make competition more effective in the hope that prices of important commodities might be brought down. It has been suggested in the report of the commission that patents on food, drugs, surgical and therapeutic devices have been used in such a way as to maintain unnecessarily high prices in these fields. I realize that many submissions have been made to the government following the publication of these reports. The government wants to consider these submissions but I would hope that at the next session of parliament appropriate action can be taken in these fields.
There is one other item to which I wish to refer and that is with regard to the work of the civil service commission in filling the vacancies in various departments. I have in my hand a very voluminous report which was tabled in this house as the result of questions which I had placed on the order paper. These questions were as follows: How many resignations have been received in each government department or crown corporation in each month in each year since January 1, 1957, from (a) professional personnel (b) administrative officers? Second, I asked: How many vacancies presently exist in each government department or crown corporation for positions to be filled by (a) professional personnel (b) administrative officers?
Now the report has been tabled in the house, and in the Department of Agriculture within this period, in the professional category there were 336 and there are still 194 vacancies. In the Department of Justice, 43 resignations, 21 vacancies still existing. In the

Department of Mines and Technical Surveys 92 resignations, 47 vacancies. In the Department of National Defence, 193 resignations, 119 vacancies. Department of National Health and Welfare, 704 resignations, 110 vacancies. Department of National Revenue, 413 resignations, 278 vacancies. Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources, 60 resignations, 25 vacancies. Department of Public Works, 71 resignations, 63 vacancies. Department of Transport, 111 resignations, 135 vacancies. Department of Veterans Affairs, 854 resignations, 223 vacancies.
Mr. Chairman, the return is not complete in that every department does not provide information as to the length of time these various vacancies have been in existence; but in looking over the information that has been given it would seem to me that there are hundreds of vacancies in the government service which have been in existence for many months.
I would ask the Acting Secretary of State to comment on why there has been such delay and apparently such difficulty in filling so many of these posts. I would think from looking over the return that perhaps the salaries which are provided in Canada for technical and professional personnel are inadequate and should be increased. It would seem to me that it must detract from the efficiency of the public service to have this very large number of vacancies apparently so difficult to fill. I would hope that speedy attention is being given to this problem. I feel that in a country like ours providing adequate and competent personnel for government departments is very essential and that these vacancies should not exist over a long period of time.
I would ask the Acting Secretary of State to give the committee any information he can as to why there are so many vacancies in existence, why apparently it has taken so long to fill them, and to say what action the government is taking or has under consideration in order to attract into the public service adequate numbers of competent and well-trained men and women.
