Mr. Chairman, I do not want to hold up the estimates of the Acting Secretary of State (Mr. Balcer), but I just want to say a few words.
I realize that earnest and sincere efforts have been made in the last three years to make Canada as a whole, and more particularly the Canadian administration, not only bilingual, but also bicultural. A striking proof of this is the simultaneous interpretation system which has been wanted by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) himself.
But as the federal administration cannot be bicultural unless it is perfectly bilingual, it is impossible not to discuss the problem of translation, a field which comes under the secretary of state.
I often complained, both in and outside the house, of the fact that not all documents, even sessional papers, reach hon. members in the French version at the same time as does the English version.
The secretary of state answered an earlier question of mine in this regard by telling me that our translators are remarkably able and quick at their task but that they are overworked. Quite obviously there should be considerably more of them. It is likewise obvious that they ought to be better paid, in the first place because they deserve it by reason of the excellence of their work and also-and this is perhaps rather more serious than it seems-because if our translators are paid more in accordance with their worth, many officials for whom and with whom they work will have much more regard for them. Those officials will look upon translators as fellow workers not merely as a necessary evil. In drafting a report, for instance, consideration could be given to the fact that the report is to be published at the

Supply-Secretary of State same time in French as in English. There would be no waiting until an hour before a document has to be tabled to realize that it should be tabled simultaneously in both the official languages of the country.
I have heard all kinds of complaints about the way the translation service is organized. No one questions the high intellectual qualifications of the heads of that service, but there are many who question their sense of organization.
I wonder if it might not be advisable to appoint, under the superintendent of translations, a manager, or whatever title might be given to the appointee, who would see that the services of better paid and more numerous translators are put to the best, most effective and most economical use in all respects.

Mr. Chairman, at the outset of my remarks, I wish to commend the Acting Secretary of State on the occasion of the appointment, as printer to Her Majesty the Queen, of Roger Duhamel, a newspaperman with extensive experience and a man who is very highly regarded in leading literary circles of the province of Quebec. It is an excellent appointment, and a wise choice. It gives me pleasure to commend the government for selecting a man of that calibre to fill this important post.
I am confident that the new Queen's printer will enjoy the respect and admiration of his entire staff.
The appointee is an upright, highly regarded man, a distinguished newspaperman who has written for many periodicals, an author with several works to his credit, and I feel sure that his appointment will be welcomed by every political party in this house.

of the cost system of the government printing bureau with that of other firms in the printing industry. I do not know whether the minister would like to listen to these questions now or if he would prefer to listen to them when the estimates for the printing bureau are before us.

Mr. Chairman, I note that this item involves an increase of $40,303, which will allow the bureau for translations to hire five more persons.

I wonder whether the number of translators is adequate to give us the service we are entitled to expect with regard to the translation of some reports.
I have noted, this year, that the French version of the Canada Year Book has been distributed six months after the English publication. The same goes for several other reports. In fact, committee reports often reach us several days, and even several weeks, after the English version has been published.
With regard to the Atlas of Canada, which was published last year, I believe the French edition came out a year after the English edition and, if I am not mistaken, the French version is out of print.
I have no doubt that our translators are efficient workers, nor do I doubt that their output is as high as it can be. That is why I say that last year, especially towards the end of the session, the health of several translators broke down. One of them suffered a stroke, and I understand that this year again some of the translators have been ordered to take a rest cure.
Therefore, could the Acting Secretary of State (Mr. Balcer) give us the assurance that we will have the French translation of the documents I have just referred to, as well as that of many others, fairly soon after the publication of the English version, especially as far as the proceedings of the committees of the House of Commons are concerned?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to reply to the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska (Mr. Boulanger), and to the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Mont-calm (Mr. Pigeon), who both dealt with the bureau for translations.
I take this opportunity to tell the house how fortunate our government and country are in having such devoted civil servants, who perform a task that is often very thankless, the translator's role being extremely important and his work most difficult.
There is no doubt that there have been regrettable delays. However, I do not think these are merely due to an inadequate number of translators on the staff, because the production of some translations is less dependent on the number of people available to do a particular job than on the division which handles it. As we know, during the session a group of excellent translators is responsible 79951-0-447J
Supply-Secretary of State for translating all the debates in the house. This work is done under pressure, and the result is that there may be delays in other services.
The hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomp-tion-Montcalm suggested a moment ago that we appoint a manager of the bureau for translations. It gives me pleasure to report to the house that we have precisely made such an appointment. Mr. Henriot Mayer has been appointed manager of the bureau for translations. His job will be to keep in touch with the various departments, so that the latter may supply the bureau for translations will all manuscripts and documents as soon as they are available. It has happened, in some cases, that a book was completely printed before it was sent to the translation service; I therefore think there is a certain amount of education to be done in some departments, it is to get them into the habit of sending their manuscripts to the translation service as soon as available so that both versions may be published at the same time.

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I want to tell the Acting Secretary of State that I am very happy to hear the good news he just announced; however, I disagree with him when he says that the present number of translators is adequate.
The appointment of a manager for the bureau for translations is a step in the right direction, but I believe that translators now employed by the department are handling more work than they can fairly be expected to handle. The new manager of the bureau for translations will possibly agree, with the least bit of encourgagement from the Acting Secretary of State and those who are familiar with prevailing conditions, that the number of translators might be substantially increased. I believe it is unfair to demand from translators the amount of work that has been demanded from them for a number of years when they have to work outside normal hours. In all positions in the civil service employees are expected to turn out an average amount of work. Now in the case of translators, or at least of a great number of them, the maximum output is demanded, and when it is a matter of translating a technical paper or professional document it is somewhat difficult to demand of those people that they work without respite, particularly under the pressure of circumstance.
Consequently, I ask the secretary of state and his new manager of the bureau for

Supply-Secretary of State translations to consider the situation and determine whether the present number of translators is really adequate.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to bring the case of Catherine Ann Meredith to the attention of the Acting Secretary of State. I read from a letter received from Letourneau, Quinlan, Forest, Emery, Raymond & Bouchard, barristers and solicitors:
Our client, after 15 years in the civil service, is being arbitrarily dismissed despite the fact of an excellent record, as attested by the copy of letter enclosed from D. R. Campbell. Esq., director of civilian personnel (navy) dated as late as December 15. 1959. Mrs. Meredith also has excellent references from the first administrative officer. Lieutenant Commander Thomas, R.C.N., retired, as well as the supervisor at Saint John, N.B., in the Department of National Revenue where our client was employed previous to coming to Montreal, in 1953.
In the circumstances, it would certainly be a shame to deprive our client of the pension which she has earned by good and faithful service over all these years, which retirement pension will become due in November, 1961.
I have a copy of a letter written to Captain J. S. Somers, R.C.N., principal naval overseer, Montreal area, dated June 23, 1960.

It is from the same lawyers. I will not read the whole letter but just some parts of it:
We note that after some 15 years of valuable experience and excellent record in the Department of National Defence, you give her less than one week, to wit: until the 27th of June, to optate for four months retiring leave beginning on August 1 and terminating on November 30, 1960 or three months cash gratuity payable on separation after November 30, 1960. From the information contained in our file, it clearly appears that our client has enjoyed an excellent record up to and including December 15, 1959, as attested by the photostatic copy of letter addressed to our client from D. R. Campbell, Esq., for the director of civilian personnel (navy).
Our client would be entitled in the normal course of events to receive her pension in the month of November, 1961. She was with the Department of National Revenue in Saint John, N.B., from the year 1945 until the year 1953. She has been in her present location with the civil service since the year 1953, adjacent to the Canadian Vickers Limited, but not connected with the latter...
Apparently, from the information contained in our file, you have sent the above letter basing yourself on article 13.02 in the civilian personnel administration and accounting manual, subsection 1 (d), which provides:
"Any employee who has attained the age of 60 years but who has not attained the age of 64 years and 6 months may be retired for reasons of age, in unusual cases where continued employment involves a serious problem."
Then there are certain matters mentioned which are not relevant. I continue:
We cannot see how these incidents could by any stretch of imagination be construed as serious problems, more particularly in view of our client's record with the department over many years.
In view of the foregoing, we do believe that it is only fair, equitable and just that our client be kept on by the department until she has reached her normal retirement age next year and be given when she is retired in November, 1961, the pension she has earned by her excellent record as any civil servant has the right to expect and get.
In view of the very short notice given, we must ask you without delay to explain the option which you set forth in your above mentioned letter, which our client does not understand.
Again, there is another letter written to me by the same firm of lawyers under date of June 30, 1960, which reads in part as follows:
I can only repeat that it does seem a shame that Captain Somers sees fit to dismiss Mrs. Meredith after all these years of good and faithful service to the Department of National Revenue and to the Department of National Defence. Especially, when she will be in the normal course of events coming of age to receive her pension next year.
In the circumstances, it seems to me that the least that they could do would be to transfer her to another department until such time as her time for pension has elapsed.
I will now read a letter from H. Thomas, lieutenant-commander (E), R.C.N., retired, no date.
I have been requested to supply a reference to the above mentioned person dealing with her duties during the period of my appointment as staff officer on the staff of the principal naval overseer, Montreal.

I will pass over some matters that are not relevant.
Mrs. Ann Meredith joined the staff in October, 1953, as a typist. Having regard to her experience and the duties required she was employed as a clerk. She worked well, with initiative and loyalty. At that time, in the circumstances, her work was invaluable. She has one highly valuable quality that fits in a technical activity-she can and does follow instructions from appropriate authority implicitly.
Observing that clerical staff can never fully understand the technical details involved, this attitude is reassuring to the responsible officer. He knows that his instructions will be carried out as required.
I also have a letter dated July 28, 1953, written by R. G. McKenna, reading as follows:
To whom it may concern:
Mrs. Catherine A. Meredith has been employed in the income tax office in Saint John, N.B., for a period of eight years. During this period she has been employed in the accounts-collections section, performing various clerical duties as well as being employed as a stenographer and typist. Her work has always proven to be very satisfactory.
I have been personally acquainted with Mrs. Meredith since July, 1951, at which time I took over the supervision of the section in which she is employed. I have found her to be a very conscientious, capable and dependable employee and believe that she will be very satisfactory. She has demonstrated that she has a considerable amount of initiative and has readily adapted herself to various new duties which she has been called upon to perform.
Then a further letter dated December 15, 1959, from D. R. Campbell for the director of civilian personnel (navy) which reads as follows:
Mr. Sharpe has requested that I forward a personal note to you expressing his regret that the authorities concerned have not found it possible to amend the civilian complement of P.N.O., Montreal, as discussed with you in his office on December 7.
In so far as your own position is concerned, the duties and responsibilities are considered to be consistent with the present classification, clerk 2. The reclassification of the other position to clerk 4 has been found to be unjustified.
It is suggested that you continue to avail yourself of every possible opportunity to enter promotional competitions in the Montreal area. By so doing it seems likely that, in due course, your valuable experience and excellent record in this department will be properly recognized and your advancement to more responsible duties will follow.
Then there is a further letter dated June 21, 1960, from J. S. Somers, captain, R.C.N., which reads as follows:
Dear Madam:
Mrs. Catherine Ann Meredith N.D.-P.N.O. 72-Clerk 2 P.N.O. Montreal
I am advised by the area civilian personnel officer that records on hand in his office indicate that you have to your credit six and a half days annual leave to which you are entitled upon separating from the service. Consequently, in order
Supply-Secretary of State to liquidate this annual leave, you will cease active duty in this office at noon hour, 21 July, 1960.
Under existing regulations and in view of your length of service, you have an option to choose either of the following:
(a)	4 months retiring leave beginning on 1 August and terminating on 30 November, 1960, or
(b)	3 months cash gratuity payable on separation after 30 November, 1960.
Observing that prior approval must be obtained from the naval secretary for either retiring leave or cash gratuity, you are hereby requested to inform me in writing of your decision before 27 June, 1960.
I believe that in the normal course of events a person who has worked 141 years for the civil service would naturally expect to receive a pension at the age of 60. This lady had worked for some 14J years and just at the time when she is looking forward to retirement on a satisfactory pension she is thanked for her services and let go. She seems to have a perfect record but after all these years she is fired from her position and asked to take some examination to see if she can qualify for some other position. If she has served the government well for 14J years I think the government should know whether she is qualified and whether she should get a pension. To say to her after all these years and just about the time she would have been eligible for a pension "We are going to let you go" seems to me to indicate that the government is trying to get away from some responsibility. They put this lady out of a job with no future in front of her on a mere whim just because they do not want to pay a pension. I should like to hear what the minister has to say about the matter.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to take a few moments of the committee's time to point out to the Acting Secretary of State a disparity between the salaries provided for some classifications and the functions those employees have to perform.
For instance, I refer to the salary scale paid certain professional classes, among others, doctors, economists, stenographers and chemists.
These are approximate figures. For instance, doctors are offered a salary of approximately $10,000 for their services.

With regard to economists, the salary offered them varies between $8,000 and $9,000; stenographers get about $6,000, whereas pharmacists are only offered some $4,500 for their professional services.
May I, Mr. Chairman, in this matter, call the minister's attention to page 38 of the civil service commission report which was published in Ottawa in December 1958, page 38 of the English text. I do not have the French version here; may I therefore quote the English text:
(Text):
4013	(ACT)
The establishment of grade levels in any class shall, within the limits set by the nature of the work to be performed, be such as to provide for a career pattern.
4014	(REG)
The commission may revise the classification or grade of any position to provide for an unusual degree of competence demonstrated by the incumbent.
(Translation):
Mr. Chairman, I hope that the Acting Secretary of State will give my remarks some favourable attention to the effect of considering the professional services of pharmacists, in the civil service; thus, I would ask him to see whether it would not be possible to increase their salaries so as to put them in line with their functions in the federal administration.
Mr. Chairman, with regard to another matter, I wish the minister would take the necessary steps to change the method of interdepartmental promotion through competition.
We know it is customary in the civil service, to have inter-service competitions for the promotion of an employee to another post; that was done in a somewhat unorthodox manner until the Conservative party took over.
May I be allowed to mention, among others, the fact that under Liberal administration, certain practices or certain undue influences were resorted to, in order to have a personal friend promoted within the civil service; thus, a special competition was prepared to give him a particular promotion in the civil service. As a matter of fact, I received some time ago a communication in this respect from an employee who had been appointed to the ordnance depot in Montreal by the former administration. Now, this gentleman, who allowed me to reveal his name here, informed me of the method used by the former administration for the purpose of promoting one of their friends. The case is that of Mr. Henry Sibley, of 7286 Musset street, Ville St. Michel, Montreal.

When a competition was advertised in the department, Mr. Sibley was approached by an official of that administration who is then supposed to have given him all the information and all the answers to the questions which were to be asked at the competition in order to allow him to get the position applied for.
Afterwards, that gentleman, wishing to be promoted, had been assured that he would be rendered the same service. Unfortunately, the necessary information could not be given, because the person who was supposed to provide it had been transferred to another department; and that gentleman could not know in advance the answers to the questions which were to be asked to those interested in taking part in the competition.
There, Mr. Chairman, you have an instance of an abject procedure which was in use and had even become prevalent under the former administration.
I am sure that the acting minister will consider it a duty to correct such an anomaly which involves an injustice towards all those who work in the civil service.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I know that bilingualism in the civil service has made great strides. And I am happy to commend the minister (Mr. Balcer) for his constant efforts to protect and emphasize the necessity of bilingualism in the federal administration.
However, I should like to call the minister's attention to the fact that a short time ago I phoned the civil service commission here in Ottawa to ask information about summer jobs for university students, and I unfortunately noted that there was no bilingual employee there to reply to the questions I wanted to ask.
I have here the name of the person concerned and the date of that occurrence and I am sure that the minister will consider it a duty and a pleasure to meet our requests.
Once again, I take this opportunity, Mr. Chairman, to congratulate the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon) and the minister for their constant efforts to establish a perfect bilingual system in the civil service.

Mr. Chairman, may I go on with my remarks in connection with the civil service commission?
Though I complained of the way in which the hon. member for St. Mary (Mr. Valade) reported some situations which arose under the former Liberal administration-as if errors were not committed under any administration-I just wanted to point out that while there had been no sign of party politics since the discussion started, I found his attitude in very bad taste; and I hope this expression is in order.
On the other hand, the hon. member made some remarks which were devoid of party politics, and which I approve. I believe he is right. He was justified in complaining of the fact that some professional civil servants are not adequately paid and that it is the reason why the civil service commission which has such great need of professional experts to carry out certain tasks, is unable to find them.
Every week, we read notices asking for accountants, and the salary offered by the civil service commission is of $3,000, $3,500 or $4,000 a year, whereas those working in
79951-0-4481
Supply-Secretary of State an accountant's office get $6,000, $7,000 and even $8,000 a year, even when they are only employees. How can the civil service commission possibly obtain the services of competent people if it fails to pay them salaries comparable to those paid in private business?
It is the same for nurses. Lately, there was a demand for a nurse to manage a hospital. She was to be sent to northern Canada, and the salary offered was the fabulous sum of $3,600 a year, to leave everything and go north. It is absurd; it is simply ridiculous.
If you want good employees, you have to pay them properly, give them salaries that are paid in private industry. I know that salaries in private industry have substantially gone up in recent years; 1 know also that it may be somewhat difficult to keep pace with salary trends everywhere, and I would not like to criticize the commission too harshly.
I remember having dealt, on another occasion, with the various job opportunities advertised by the civil service, when I showed that it had been difficult to find the required personnel for hundreds of positions, precisely because the salary offered was not reasonable.
As I said a moment ago, the same goes for accountants and nurses and, as the hon. member for St. Mary pointed out, the same goes for druggists and chemists. It is true that chemists are classified in various categories. At the very beginning, a chemist only gets about $3,000 a year, and it is only after constant labour and years of work that he can get a reasonable salary. Besides, if he is competent, he goes to work for a company like the C.I.L. and right away he is offered a high salary.
Canada is now losing several of its doctors precisely because they do not get adequate salaries. In fact, American professionals have called at our universities, and even before our medical students had received their degree, they were offered a remuneration so much higher than that which they could have got in Canada, that those young people went to the United States to complete their studies and, afterwards, they settled there.
We have also seen a California lecturer come to Toronto and Montreal to give lectures to our doctors. This lecturer was a Canadian who had emigrated to the United States because he could not get the necessary facilities to work, and the salary which would

Supply-Secretary of State have allowed him to complete his education. He is now a United States citizen, and he comes back to Canada to lecture our Canadians.
Mr. Chairman, I believe that in this field the civil service commission would do well to make a serious and thorough study of the situation in order to meet the needs of the civil service and to give satisfaction also to those who, because of their education, deserve to get a salary at least equal to that they would receive in industry.
Mr. Chairman, I would also like to deal with the matter of appeals to the civil service commission. It is a situation which should be seriously examined, because many of the appeals are rejected. Why? It is because the civil service commission is not giving serious enough consideration to those who make an appeal? I do not know, but in the few cases I have studied, I have noticed that the civil servant, who was a very good employee, fully qualified for the work he had to do, did not get the appointment to the higher position he had applied for. The promotion has been refused to him in favour of another civil servant. He filed an appeal. He appeared before the commission and his appeal was fruitless. Why? Because he was naturally shy and did not have the necessary knowledge to plead his case. This is why I believe that in cases of appeal-I am now talking for the benefit of lawyers-the applicant should have the right to be represented by a lawyer, who would know how to make the necessary representations to the commission and would know how to examine the witnesses.
Otherwise, the man who is not used to speaking up, who did not make special studies in that field is stuck; he is embarrassed because he is not used to expressing his views publicly. He is terrorized by the presence of the members of the civil service commission, and, for those reasons, he often loses his appeal simply because he does not know how to go about it.
Mr. Chairman, I suggest that the civil service commission take steps so that those who make an appeal have the right, if they so choose, not to be represented by another employee of the public service, nor by a member of his association, but by a lawyer of his choice.
Another field where there is some injustice, perhaps unintentional, is in what we call the


rating system. The rating is a survey made by the department concerned, on the value of the employee. They say, for instance, that the employee is worth so much per cent in this and so much per cent in that and at the end, it should give a total of so much.
But in the army, they instituted the rating system. The rating was shown to the person concerned who considered the matter, and if dissatisfied, asked to be paraded in order to discuss the situation.
Things are different in the civil service commission. The head of a department-

I am sorry I was going too fast. In the civil service, the person concerned is treated the same as in the army. I do know, however, that an employee's rating is arrived at on the basis of a numerical system and that outside the Department of National Defence, which has been following a system similar to the army system, an employee is not given an opportunity to see his rating. Now, in the event of a promotion, the rating has more weight than the person's real value. In my view, the employee should be told about his rating, so as to be able to study it and appeal to the civil service commission if he disagrees; if satisfied, on the other hand, he could just initial the rating. In that way, no unfairness could arise.
I have referred to that system in the past. I discussed it when the Liberals were in power, and I raise it again today because in my view, it is a means of avoiding cases of gross unfairness. Indeed, it may happen that a head of a division, who for some reason dislikes a particular employee, will rate him accordingly. As the employee never sees that rating, and comes under the civil service commission only when a promotion arises, his chances are jeopardized in advance because of the fact that in a fit of temper against an employee, the section head does not grant him the rating he is entitled to.
Those are matters that deserve consideration as well as the question raised earlier by the hon. member for Outremont-St. Jean (Mr. Bourque).
Mistakes might happen, the civil service commission may do someone an injustice; but the greatest danger of injustice is not in the civil service commission itself, but mostly in the departments where people work side by side all day long and where there

are clashes of temperaments. Those people do not always get along together and this is what gives rise to injustice, because very often reports submitted to the civil service commission on applicants have more weight than the true merit of the applicants and are more important than the results of the exams they passed. I suggest that this situation should be corrected in the interests of the civil service.

It is a charge against the civil service of Canada as a whole and more particularly against the chairmen of the civil service commission who have occupied that post over the years. The charge made was that an applicant for a position in the civil service of Canada was given the questions and answers with respect to an examination which took place. Mr. Heeney, now ambassador at Washington, who was appointed by the former Liberal administration and whose term of office was extended by the present government. If the charge is a valid one then it reflects indirectly upon his tenure of office. Again, his predecessor in office was Mr. C. H. Bland, who for many years was chairman of the civil service commission. He was appointed by a Conservative administration and his term of office was extended by a Liberal administration. Before his retirement he was asked to make a report on the whole purview of the civil service commission.
What I deprecate in this attack is not so much the fact that it is directed at a previous administration but rather the fact that it is an attack upon the civil service commission of Canada. I have been a member of the house for many years. I came here in 1935 and I have heard silly rumours such as that to which the hon. member for St. Mary gave vent this evening, but I have never yet seen the proof established of any such thing as was stated this evening. I say to you, sir, with respect, and equally with respect to the Acting Secretary of State, that it is not enough for him to say what he did say. In

all fairness to the men and women who are under him he must say that they are not in any way responsible so far as this kind of ignoble attack is concerned. I hope the minister will conduct an investigation at the first opportunity and let the house know what the facts of the case are.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I explained briefly that the figures that were given by the hon. member were not the actual figures for vacancies. They include all the people who have resigned from the civil service because of retirement, because of age, because of illness, because of marriage in the case of women, to fill alternative positions such as returning to universities and schools, as well as for personal reasons of some other nature. When you take into consideration these various groups you will see that the actual resignations are not so numerous for such a huge service.
In so far as these vacancies are concerned, the commission has experienced shortages in certain fields, such as veterinarians, nurses, meteorologists and accountants. Industry is also experiencing shortages in these classes. I can assure the hon. member that our civil service commission is doing its best to recruit these people.

My main point was not the number of resignations. The point was that in relation to resignations there were so many vacancies. I have in my hand a particular return for the Department of Agriculture. For example in two instances the position of engineer has been vacant one year and one month; two veterinarians have been required for this length of time; two librarians, an inspector of poultry products, a poultry field-man. The position of economist has been vacant one year and five months, and so on. It would seem to me that there has been something of a collapse in the civil service of this country in these important positions. The fact is that the government is not offering enough money, in my opinion. Some of these positions have been vacant for years.

Supply-Secretary of State
I am not criticizing the civil service commission for failing to have them filled. I think the personnel are not available at the salaries that are being offered. My complaint, as I said initially, was not the number of resignations. I expect there will be a large turnover, inevitably, in any service because of promotions, transfers, new recruits and so on. As I said earlier, I do not have the full information because it was not supplied for every department. I would ask the minister to look into this question. I feel that it is a very great problem for the civil service of this country, and it is a shame that these positions should be vacant for years. I would suggest that one of the reasons the government is unable to fill them is that the salary which is offered for people with these kinds of qualifications is too low.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am told by the officials that there is an actual shortage of veterinarians, for instance, and they are just not available. In so far as many of the other positions are concerned that the hon. member has listed, very often the department concerned does not request the civil service commission to fill these vacancies. The department just wants to keep these positions open.
Why would the department want to keep them open?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: That is the problem of the various departments; so far as the civil service commission is concerned, they only recruit people to fill vacancies when the *department requests that these vacancies be filled.

I did not expect to hear from the minister that these were fictitious vacancies. 1 think it is a rather disgraceful position if the Department of Agriculture is going about the country saying we have many vacancies; we need a number of qualified people for many posts, but we do not want these posts filled. It looks ridiculous.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Many of these vacancies remain unfilled because applicants do not come.
Very well; in other words, in relation to the salary there is a severe shortage of these people and the government is unsuccessful in having these positions filled.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: At the present time the government is granting all kinds of salary increases. A few minutes ago I listed a group of professional men who received increases on June 1, quite substantial increases. I feel these increases compare quite favourably with the salaries paid in industry for similar work.

There are some vacancies in the Department of Agriculture, and the hon. member for Assiniboia is a trained agriculturist. I sincerely recommend to the minister that he consider an application from the hon. member for Assiniboia in order that he may use his great talents in a field outside this house.
I suggest to the hon. member that my application is in for much higher stakes than that.
Oh, oh.

I suggest that the record of inefficiency and ineptitude of this government will result in innumerable vacancies on the other side. My hon. friend's advice, I would suggest, would be more appropriate to the droves of his colleagues around him who, in a very short time, will likely all be looking for work.

I was going to ask the minister a question related to one of his own divisions. Has the civil service commission any request from the companies division of his department for additional staff, especially in relation to the carrying out of what will be great changes in the functions of that division if the present dealings with the provinces in an effort to smooth out the whole Companies Act operation in Canada should be successful.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I cannot answer that question offhand; I shall be obliged to inquire. Perhaps I could let the hon. member know personally outside the house with regard to this matter because I do not think I can get an answer tonight.

That will be satisfactory. Will the minister also let me know at what time it is expected that some kind of crystallization will take place on this program to consolidate the various provincial and federal companies acts across the country and when he expects that this program will have some kind of policy application?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I could not tell exactly how many months it may take. This process is a long one, as the hon. member knows. At the present time this committee, which consists of representatives of the federal companies section and a representative of each of the companies law section of the various provinces, is preparing a joint draft to be submitted to the government of each province and of Canada. If I remember rightly, this draft at the present time has not been given to the government and the government has not considered such a draft at the present time. I do not know about the various provinces but I do not think the matter has reached the government level. I believe it is

still on the official level, or on the level of this committee of which I was speaking. However, I can assure the hon. member that when we have uniformity of companies law across the country, if there is a need to increase the number of officers in the companies law section of the department, we shall do so.
Can the minister inform the committee whether there is at the present time an active chief or an acting chief of the companies branch?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: We have only an acting chief at the present time.
How long has the position of chief of the department been vacant?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I am not too sure but I think it is over five months; between five months and six months.
Has the minister taken under active consideration the appointment of a chief for that department? I know the department is in need of a chief.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Yes. We want to fill this vacancy. At the present time we are discussing the matter with the civil service commission.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Public printing and stationery-
320. Departmental administration, $675,523.

On a previous occasion when these estimates have been before a committee I made a request of the minister to use his influence to see that contracts were spread out more across the country or in other words that there be less concentration in the Mont-real-Toronto-Ottawa triangle and on at least two occasions, once by the present Minister of Citizenship and Immigration and once by the minister who was in charge of this section last year, I received the assurance that this was the policy of the government and that they were going to see to it that more contracts and subcontracts went to the western provinces and to some of the eastern provinces. I should like to ask the minister whether he can give some indication as to whether this policy has been effective.
In previous years I put on the order paper a request for information that it took many pages to give. However, from it I can determine this information. Last year in this particular return I could not see that more contracts were going to provinces other than Ontario and Quebec. I wonder whether the minister could give us an indication now as to what increase there has been, perhaps in percentage terms, of contracts going to printers in Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta, British Columbia and the maritime provinces?
Supply-Secretary of State

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I am glad the hon. member has asked me this question because the figures that I can give at the present time show quite a definite increase. For instance, in Alberta in 1957-58 the total value of departmental purchases from the Queen's printer was $55,014; in 1958-59 the amount increased to $75,451; and in 1959-60 it has reached $83,018. In British Columbia, for instance, it was $110,000 in 1957-58; in 1958-59 it stayed at about the same level of $108,000; but in 1959-60 it increased from $108,000 to $164,000, which is quite substantial for British Columbia. With regard to Manitoba the amount increased from $80,000 in 1957 to $137,000 in 1959-60.

I should just like the minister to give the pattern. I appreciate knowing the figures. Has there been any percentage increase over-all in these particular years that would indicate that we are just following a general trend? I should like to determine whether this is following a general trend or whether it is a real fruition of a change in government policy.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: If one looks at the total record, it will be seen that in 1957 the total sales were $17,400,000. The figure increased in 1958, one year later, to $18,330,000 and in 1959-60 to $18,400,000 which is an increase of only $100,000. I therefore think there is a definite movement of decentralization.

I am pleased to have this indication of a change in policy. Will the minister indicate how much of this $18 million is put up for bid, where you have an open bid or an open tender? I should like the figure, roughly, as to how much is on the basis of a selective invitation to a few people who happen to be on the list of the department?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: It is practically all open bids. The only cases in which there are no open bids are in respect of these punch cards or specialized equipment like that which are produced by only one producer and where there is only one firm from which they can be purchased.

How does a job printing firm in a small town in northern Ontario like Geraldton or a town like Brandon or Selkirk in Manitoba know, find out or hear about these tender possibilities in order that they might submit a bid?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
They are invited by area. Every time there is a printing contract to be let we always invite a certain number of printing shops to tender. As I understand it, the Queen's printer has a list of practically all printing shops in Canada. Any printing

Supply-Secretary of State shop can write to the Queen's printer giving its name, qualifications and details of its production possibilities, and the Queen's printer tries to encourage all printing shops in Canada to submit tenders, and the Queen's printer tries to give a chance to the printing shops in one particular area. It would be practically impossible for a printer in Brandon, for instance, to compete with a printer in Ottawa or Montreal or Toronto on account of shipping charges, and things like that. So we arrange to have these bids submitted by area, and that is the reason why in the last three years there has been an increase in contracts granted outside of the central provinces.

Could the minister tell me if there have been any contracts let in the past year in the area I call northwestern Ontario, which is between the Manitoba boundary down to North Bay or Sudbury? Have there been any contracts let in that area; or if that question cannot be answered, have firms in that region been invited to make bids?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: In view of the importance of cities like Port Arthur and Fort William I am sure that there are some printing firms there which have been asked to tender on contracts, but unfortunately I have not the breakdown for the region specified by the hon. member.
One last question, and this is more specific. How much does it cost, and who is the printer who does the job on the Canadian army journal?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: The successful tenderer was Charters of Brantford, Ontario. Unfortunately I have not the amount.
Can the minister tell me how many firms bid or were invited to bid on this particular job, and did the lowest bidder get the job?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: At least a dozen printing shops were asked to tender, and the hon. member can be sure the contract was given to the lowest tenderer.
I thank the minister for the information. It does not match with what I have but I will have to check my information.
In those cases do they call for public tenders or do they just call certain firms?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
What is being done in practice is that we call for a specified job according to the equipment of the various tenderers. I mean by that that for a definite printing job which requires a certain type of printing

press we call for tenders from various printing shops where they have the required press.
That is what we call invited tenders. By which means do they establish that they are better equipped than other firms to do the job? Who makes the inquiry about that?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Nobody decides which is better equipped. The various printing shops send to the Queen's printer details of all their equipment, and it is very easy for the Queen's printer to be able to judge from the equipment on the card if a particular printing shop can do a certain type of work or not.
Anybody who has good equipment can send a demand for work at the printing bureau and they would be put on the list and asked to tender?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Yes; and I can assure the hon. member that we receive requests like that every day and all of them are considered for tenders.

As I said previously, Mr. Chairman, I have a lot of questions to ask. I am a printer by trade, and therefore when you talk to me about printing, after having spent some 50 years in the trade, I have learned a lot of things in that time.
The evolution which has taken place in the printing industry during the last few years is so tremendous that it would be difficult for anyone to call it an evolution. When tenders are asked for by the printing bureau, if you want to have cheap tenders you could ask ten people and know before you start which one will be the lowest. Because the machinery is such today that certain printers can turn out a job at say, $1.94 a thousand, yet you can ask another big printer equipped with the most modern equipment possible and he can turn out the same job for about 46 cents a thousand, a difference of 75 per cent. So therefore I am sure the printing bureau has a list of all firms in Canada with the equipment they possess, and I am sure they would ask ten printers having similar up-to-date equipment to tender so that they will get the best price. I would like to ask the minister if this is so?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Would the hon. member repeat his question, because I was disturbed and missed part of it?

I will give an illustration of my question. Say the government wanted 500,000 dodgers 9 x 12 printed in two colours and two sides. If they asked a small printer with automatic machines, say Kelly presses, he will give you a price of, say, $2.25 a thousand and that will be a fair price

for him. But if you asked a big lithographic printer which had all the modern and latest type presses, his price would be perhaps only 75 per cent of the other price. So I think the printing bureau should have a list of all firms in Canada with the equipment each firm has, and they should ask similar firms with similar equipment to tender, because the difference in cost can be tremendous.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, I understand the question. We divide the various orders up into three categories; small, medium and large. With the small printing shops we ask them to tender on the smaller contracts. The huge, big concerns are invited to tender on the really big contracts. We understand the situation pictured by the hon. member and he can be sure that the Queen's printer is very much in the know as regards this situation. That is why they always divide these contracts into three classes, and when we ask for bids on a small contract we always ask the small printing shops.

As I said earlier I was led to ask these questions after reading an address given to the employing printers' association of Montreal on June 8, 1960 by David MacLellan, general manager of E.P.A. and of the graphic arts industries association, a national body embracing all employing printers' organizations from coast to coast entitled, "Printing-Canada's Biggest Employer in Manufacturing and How the Industry is Taxed, Trammelled and Trimmed".
My first question is this. Are the salaries of the officials-the Queen's printer, his assistant and other officials-paid by the government printing bureau or are they included in the civil service and paid by the government?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the Queen's printer and his assistant are paid out of the vote in the estimates but all the production people are paid out of revenues from our sales and charged to expenses.
I am sorry, but I did not hear the answer.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: As far as the Queen's printer and his assistant are concerned they are paid out of the vote in the present estimates. As far as the production people are concerned they are paid out of general expenses and charged to the cost of jobs.

Are these the only two officials paid from the estimates or are the salaries of other officials added on to the hourly cost, because the hourly cost has a great bearing on printing costs and estimates. If only the two are paid from the estimate it does not amount to much but
Supply-Secretary of State there may be other officials who are not on the payroll of the printing bureau.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I do not quite appreciate what the hon. member is after. Does he want to know, for instance, if there are people other than the officials whose salaries are charged to the ordinary expenses of this department?

Right. I want to know what officials, employees and staff are paid out of the estimates. Is it only the Queen's printer and his assistant or are the proofreaders, the chief accountant, the accountants and other officials included? What other officials are there that should be on the payroll included in the estimates or paid directly through the printing bureau and do they count on the hourly cost?
Consult page 426 of the estimates.
It is all on the first item.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: It would be difficult for me to tell exactly because some do and some do not. It depends on the work being done.
You have your officials there, Mr. Minister. Why can they not tell you? They should be able to tell you. It has a great bearing on what I have to say.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: If the hon. member will refer to page 426 of the estimates he will see that the Queen's printer and his assistant-
Do all of these officials come under the vote?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I apologize for giving the hon. gentleman incorrect information. At page 426 are listed all the people who are paid out of the vote. All the other employees of the Queen's printer, and there are over 1,500 of them, are paid out of the ordinary expenses.
That is the operating staff, the typesetters, the pressmen, all the people working in the offices of the department? Their salary is charged against the hourly cost of the printing bureau?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, and also the production men, the planning manager, the planning clerk, the storekeepers, the shipping employees and various others.
Did the minister say creative men? Did he say he has a creative staff in the printing bureau and that they create all kinds of ideas?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I did not mention that. I referred to the shipping employees. Perhaps the hon. member misunderstood me.

Supply-Secretary of State

Who purchases the necessary equipment such as presses, flat-bed and offset presses, linotype and monotype machines, gathering machines, varitypers, Xerox, I.B.M. equipment, collating and cutting machines, bookbinding equipment, etc.? Who pays for this equipment? Is it paid for and charged directly as an overhead expense in the printing bureau or is the cost of these machines calculated as overhead and included in the hourly cost of operations?
See page 437.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: All these expenses are included in vote No. 326 covering plant equipment and replacements.
Do you charge depreciation on this equipment?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: No.
An ordinary printer could not very well operate unless he charged depreciation.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: This is not an ordinary printing shop.
This is the Queen's printer.

Years ago we used to buy a press and try to make it last for 20 years but now competition is so keen that a press should be operated 24 hours a day and worked until it is absolutely through. That is the only way you can operate a printing plant today.
Who pays for the lighting, heating, maintenance, etc.? Is it charged to the printing bureau and has it got any bearing on the cost of operations? In other words, does it form part of the actual hourly cost?
If you know, why ask all these questions?
I have to ask them. The hon. member obviously knows nothing about business.

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext: If you know so much why not help them at the printing bureau?
I am not interested in working there.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Anyone who is a little familiar with government operations in the cities of Ottawa and Hull is aware of the fact that this building was constructed by the Department of Public Works and is heated by that department.
No rental is charged that goes on the hourly cost?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
None. The Department of Public Works looks after this building as it looks

after the House of Commons. The House of Commons is not charged rental.

That is what I wanted to know and that is what the printers of Canada wanted to know. What department is the rental value of the printing bureau charged to? Is it charged to a specific department or is it just an overhead charge that adds nothing to the hourly cost of operation? Does the cost of the building enter into the hourly cost of operation? Is any rental included in that cost?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: The printing bureau, like other similar establishments of the government of Canada, operates under the same rules applying to them.
It is unique. There is nothing like it.

There is a difference. I should like the minister to tell me if the delivery of printing to the various government departments, the cost of automobiles and trucks and other equipment, is included as overhead? Who pays for that?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: The charges for operating expenses of the trucks are charged to the operating expenses of the Queen's printer.
Does this go on the estimate or does it go on the hourly cost?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: On the hourly cost.

Does the printing bureau pay a municipal tax for its building or is the tax included with the stipulated amount the government pays to municipalities? If so, is there any charge made for this item to the printing bureau?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: No. The hon. member is seeking to make out a case to illustrate that the Queen's printer has not the same charges as an ordinary printing shop. We all agree with him; we have not the same charges. It is a completely different establishment. It is a government establishment created to print government publications and it is doing a very good job at the present time.

I did not ask that; I did not say it was not doing a good job. I just want information. After all, the printing bureau does not pay for lighting; it does not pay for heating; it does not pay for the building. It has no overhead costs, or anything. Is it charged any income tax?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: No, it does not pay any income tax.

If it succeeds in making a profit in competition with private industry, why should it not pay income tax, the same

as any private printer who has to pay for all the services that the printing bureau is granted by the different departments such as public works, national revenue division, and so forth?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. member has been asking so many questions of me about this matter that I wonder whether he would answer one for me?
Yes.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Does he think the printing bureau should pay income tax?

I think it should if it is going to be in competition with private industry and the printers who are competing with it right along. They have to pay rent, light, heat, and so on. That is exactly the question I wanted the minister to ask me. The private printers who are in competition with the printing bureau have to pay for rent, light, heat, maintenance, delivery, promotion, advertising, taxes of all sorts, wages, salaries, legal expenses and so forth. I can assure the minister that the printers are very much worried at the present time because of the work that the printing bureau is doing in Canada today. The printing bureau has no sales staff going to the different departments to find out what work needs to be done, or is the work brought to the printing bureau? The printing bureau has no public relations officials, no creative division of artists and top executives who create all kinds of mailing pieces, packagings, labels, promotional work, and so forth, for the different departments? Therefore, the overhead is reduced practically to wages only.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: And materials.

And materials, of course; you have to buy the materials. How is the hourly cost arrived at in the printing bureau? If you wish to estimate a job and you want to get out 500,000 booklets for tourists and the job is worth say $25,000 or $35,000 and you ask for bids outside, what do you do? I believe you have an estimating department in the printing bureau which says that the job should be worth so much. If you do not pay any overhead, and you do not pay any income tax, and you do not pay lawyers' fees and you get a free building, free light, a president, a vice president, a superintendent, a foreman and everybody, and nothing is charged on the job, how can you come to a price that is competitive with that of a printer who has to pay all those charges?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
The Queen's printer does not have to pay income tax; he does not have to pay selling expenses; he does not have
Supply-Secretary of State any depreciation and he does not make a profit. The formula that they use in assessing the price of a certain job is that they subtract 36 per cent for the cost of the printing job.
I did not get that.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: They subtract 36 per cent from the cost of the printing job. Their regulation is that this 36 per cent is to represent the fact that there is no charge for profit, for income tax, for selling expenses or for depreciation.
They do not know whether it is right or wrong.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: They do.
They start and finish-

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I cannot let that go. They have made accounting studies and they have come up with a figure of 36 per cent. It did not come out of thin air. They take the usual expenses of an ordinary printing shop and with those figures they have come up with the exact percentage of 36 per cent, and that is how they come to their costs.

Mr. Chairman, take the case of the working man an ordinary compositor in a plant who may be paid $1.98 an hour. He has two weeks' holidays, some have three. There are so many legal holidays a year and there is so much sick leave and everything. By the time you figure all the costs of that man-I am not saying the unproductive time but the productive time-that rate of $1.98 an hour may rise to $2.48 before you even begin to add profit or anything. How can you come up with a figure of 36 per cent if you do not know just where you are starting, from? In bookkeeping you must start with a figure; you do not guess and say we take 36 per cent off.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I know the hon. member is trying to make a point and I am ready to agree with him that it is less expensive for the Queen's printer to operate than it is for an ordinary printer, but as far as the costs that we charge are concerned, they are the same as those of any other printer. I referred to the cost system.

I can tell the minister that if he were in private enterprise and running a private firm he could take a job today for approximately $10,000 and it might cost him $18,000 to turn it out. The next day he might take a job for $15,000 and it may cost him only $12,000 to turn it out. At the end of the year he might arrive at a figure something like the 36 per cent that the

Supply-Secretary of State minister has mentioned, but I do not understand how the printing bureau can arrive at a figure of 36 per cent unless they start with something. You must have a firm figure. You cannot afford to guess at something; you have to know where you are going to land.
Mr. Chairman-
Wait a minute, I am not finished. Is the hon. member rising on a question of privilege?
No, I have a question.

I am not finished. I should like to ask a question about apprentices. Does the printing bureau train apprentices, or does it absorb apprentices trained by free enterprise as fast as they become journeymen? It costs a printing firm thousands of dollars to train apprentices. According to the rules, a printing firm can have only three apprentices. Out of every three apprentices who start in the printing business only one finishes. Does the printing bureau train its own apprentices, or does it take apprentices that private printers have trained? Does it recruit apprentices from those people who have trained them, and bring them into the printing bureau?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: We recruit from technical schools.
Did the government of Canada operate the printing bureau during the years 1935 to 1957? I should also like to ask the minister if there has been any change in the method of valuation since 1957.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: No, it is exactly the same as when the government of the party to which the hon. member for Outremont-St. Jean belongs was in power.
You mean you have not been able to find any method of improving it since?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: We have changed the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
We did not lose as much money.
(Translation):

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I realize that the hon. member for Outremont-St. Jean (Mr. Bourque) is very interested in the matter, and I simply wanted to ask him, as a recently elected member, who has only been here since 1957, and who needs to gain some experience, whether he would explain the difference between the former Liberal policy in this field and that of the party now in power.

I can tell the hon. member that I have been here longer than he has.


I have been sitting through four different parliaments, so that 1 have a little more experience than he has.
(Text):
I should like to ask another question. I have not received a reply so far as printers are concerned. No doubt the minister knows, as I said, that master printers spend thousands of dollars and the government should not take advantage of the printing industry by taking from them the apprentices that they train. Does the minister not think it is a grave injustice to the printing industry to take these apprentices from them?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I certainly do not think so; I do not think it is an injustice at all. I think the Queen's printer is an establishment that is rendering a tremendous service to the people of Canada. It is producing for the government of Canada and its agencies and if it can operate at a low cost I think that is a splendid thing. If we can save money for the taxpayers of Canada that is a very good thing.
The government should not take advantage of the printers by raiding their establishments to get staff. It should form its own staff.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I do not agree.

Does the minister know that the graphic arts are first among Canadian manufacturing industries in employment and fourth in dollar value of production? From the standpoint of income taxes, the graphic arts industry pays the highest wages of any non-seasonal manufacturing industry and the amount of income tax paid by the employees is considerable. Does the minister not think that the government should not cripple the goose that lays the golden egg by competing with private industry unless it be on the same level? Does the minister not think that the minister should take into consideration all the items that enter into the cost of a finished job in the printing industry before presenting competitive cost figures from the government printing bureau that show only one half of the real cost?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. member has been asking me the same questions over and over and over again.
No, I have asked different questions.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: He has repeated himself about five times and his last question is the same.
I have not.

speechtext:
I do not agree with him and I still maintain that this establishment is not creating trouble for the printing industry in Canada but rather is rendering a great

I would say to the minister-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Burnaby-Richmond.

Mr. Chairman, I think the minister might like a little variety in the questioning. Under this item I should like to make a plea primarily for the benefit of the judges and lawyers of Canada and it has to do with the printing of the annual statutes of Canada. Last year, for example, the session ended on July 18 and yet I was not able to obtain the statutes of Canada until the beginning of January. Out of curiosity I went to the library of the Supreme Court of Canada. When they receive the statutes they stamp them and I found that an interval of six to eight months was the average over several years.
I believe that one of the most important things parliament does is to enact legislation and in my view it is important that we place the statutes, comprising new legislation and amendments to existing acts, in the hands of the judges and lawyers of Canada as soon as possible. I believe it is extremely important that they receive them with the greatest expedition. I am not being critical of the minister or the Queen's printer because I realize they have a variety of matters to attend to but I do not think it is right that the judges and lawyers of Canada should be in the position of not knowing what the up-to-date law is. I urge the minister to expedite, if possible, the printing of this very important publication and I suggest that perhaps it could be done in a period of two months.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. member has asked a very refreshing question and has made a very sound suggestion. I think it is most important that the statutes of Canada should be printed as quickly as possible because they play an important part in Canadian life. I can assure the hon. member that we will take his remarks and suggestion under very serious consideration and will do our utmost to complete the printing of these statutes earlier this year.

Mr. Chairman, I must confess I have been quite amazed and rather confused by the running battle we have seen tonight between the hon. member for Outremont-St. Jean and the minister. My confusion arises from the fact that I cannot
Supply-Secretary of State make out whether this is the new liberalism of the Conservative party or the new conservatism of the Liberal party. However, one thing strikes me as very strange. It has been repeated many times by the hon. member that the Queen's printer competes with private printing companies. I do not know of one instance where the Queen's printer has gone out and competed with any printing company in Canada. I think his whole argument is based on a myth.

May I ask the minister another question? Does he know that our small population supports the greatest volume of imported printing of any country in the world? Sixty per cent of United States printing exports are absorbed by Canada and only 5 per cent of our printing exports are absorbed by the United States. We absorb 60 per cent of printing exports manufactured by 170 million people and they only absorb 5 per cent of printed material manufactured by 17 million people. If it were 5 per cent to 60 per cent the situation would not be so bad, but it is like an elephant and a rabbit or comparing 60,000 elephants we take from them with 5,000 rabbits they take from us. In addition, I understand that the Japanese are now coming into the market.
I am sorry if I have annoyed the minister but these are all things that the printing fraternity are very anxious to know. As we have a new Queen's printer I thought it would be well to make him aware of the things he will have to put up with and that is why I have asked so many questions tonight. I can assure him I wish him well and I hope he will make a success of his new job. I hope he will also take the things I have said tonight into consideration and try to bring about a fair distribution of the woi'k that he gives out.

I have one question which I have been waiting quite a while to ask. Would the minister inform the house who prints the Parliamentary Guide and, if it is printed privately, what is the name of the company and what do they charge for it?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: It is strictly private. The copies that we have are bought by the House of Commons, and it is the commissioners of internal economy that do that.
The right to print is given by the commissioners?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
It is purely private. It has been done by the same family for quite a

Supply-Secretary of State number of years. The copies are bought by the commissioners of internal economy of the house.
